news.title: Is America Ready for a Gay President?
news.text:
During an appearance on NBC's Meet the Press, host Kristen Welker asked Buttigieg about his blatantly obvious presidential ambitions. She asked him directly whether America was truly ready to elect a gay president, bringing up what Kamala Harris’s ghostwriter wrote in her memoir.

“I do want to talk a bit about your political future, Mr. Secretary,” Welker began. “Former Vice President Kamala Harris wrote in her book about the 2024 election that you came close to being her running mate. Let me remind people of this passage. She writes of the eight names on the list for vetting. ‘I might as well say that Pete Buttigieg was my first choice. He would have been an ideal partner if I were a straight white man. But knowing what was at stake, it was too big of a risk.’ She was essentially saying that she didn’t think America was ready for a gay vice president with a black woman at the top of the ticket. Let me ask you today, do you think America is ready for a gay president?”

As you might expect, Buttigieg didn't hedge.

"I wouldn't have run for president in the first place if I didn't believe that," he insisted. "Of course."

And then he kept talking.

"My experience in South Bend, Indiana, getting re-elected with 80% of the vote after coming out, and my experience right now traveling the country shows me that what's really on people's minds isn't about you, your identity as a candidate," he continued. "It's about them. It's about their lives."

Welker then asked him whether he'd commit to running in 2028, even though it is pretty obvious he’s planning to run. "I don't think now is the time to even be talking about that," he said. "I think by my count, we've been to 35 states since I left the cabinet."

NEW: Democrat Pete Buttigieg says America is ready for a gay president. https://t.co/tfdEogpXKW— Collin Rugg (@CollinRugg) September 14, 2026

He happened to be in New Mexico at the time, a state that falls on the early presidential primary calendar — some coincidence.

Recommended: What This Clancy Juror Admitted to Is the Worst Revelation Yet

Buttigieg clearly understands what Kamala's calculus proved. A gay identity is an asset inside today's Democrat base. Why? Because Democrats thrive on identity politics, and every national ticket for twenty years has carried some kind of "historic first" as a gimmick. In 2008, it was that Barack Obama would have been the first black man elected president. In 2016, Hillary Clinton would have been the first woman elected president. In 2020, Kamala became the first female vice president. In 2024, she would have been the first female president.

At this rate, every Democrat ticket going forward will feature a woman or a minority somewhere on it.

So the identity-politics box has been checked plenty of times already. The open question is whether America will check the one Buttigieg is banking on: an openly gay man in the Oval Office.

I'm not sold that it will. Yes, America's views on same-sex marriage and homosexuality have shifted dramatically over the last 30 years, and Buttigieg himself doesn't scare anyone. He was a lousy transportation secretary, but he comes across as a normal guy. The trouble starts once you get past the B in LGBTQ+ and into the T and the Q and whatever the plus is, and recent polling shows Americans swinging against mutilation of children, the unfairness of letting biological men compete in women's sports, and all that nonsense about there being more than two genders.

Buttigieg didn't build that brand, but guess what? He's stuck carrying it. And until voters stop associating the TQ+ with the LGB, a gay president isn't happening, no matter how many states he visits or how normal he seems.
news.author: Matt Margolis

news.title: Gavin Newsom reveals he won’t run for president in 2028 if a certain other Democrat does
news.text:
California Governor Gavin Newsom has revealed that he won’t run for president in 2028 if former Vice President Kamala Harris does. 

Newsom is considered a top potential Democratic candidate in the next presidential election, which is a little more than two years away. While the governor is still weighing a potential run, he told CNN’s Jake Tapper in a new interview that he wouldn’t throw his hat in the ring if Harris was in the race. 

“I wouldn’t run if she ran,” Newsom said while fly fishing in Montana with Tapper as part of a series where the news anchor chats with politicians in some of their favorite places. “Why would I? I wouldn’t do that to her. I wouldn’t do that to you. I wouldn’t waste everyone’s time.”

When Tapper asked Newsom to explain, the governor suggested that pitting two California Democrats against each other would force their shared base to choose between them, handing an advantage to the other candidates. 

“Electorally, it’s a gift from God for everybody else. They’d enjoy the hell out of it — mutual assured destruction. It services no greater good,” Newsom said. 

The governor endorsed Harris when former President Joe Biden dropped out of the 2024 presidential election, writing on X, “With our democracy at stake and our future on the line, no one is better to prosecute the case against Donald Trump’s dark vision and guide our country in a healthier direction than [Harris].” 

Newsom, who has gained popularity during Donald Trump’s second term for mocking the president online, also has five other people to consider when deciding to run in 2028 — his wife, Jennifer Siebel Newsom, and their four kids. 

“I know what matters in life,” Newsom told Tapper in a clip of their interview, which will air in full Tuesday. “I’ve got four kids. It’s the only thing that matters to me. They gotta be on board.”

When Politico’s Jonathan Martin asked Newsom in a March interview whether his kids would want him to run for president, the governor said, “It depends on the day of the week.”

Newsom then told a story of his teenage son asking him about running in 2028.

When Newsom denied that he had decided on a presidential bid, his son said, “Good.” The California governor then asked him what he meant by that, and his son replied, “We’re too young and you need to spend more time with us.”

Other names widely floated as potential Democratic candidates in 2028 are progressive congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Biden’s Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, who ran for president in 2020. 

In a Bowling Green State University/YouGov poll of likely voters released earlier this month, Harris received 17 percent of support for the Democratic nomination and Newsom received 14 percent. 

Buttigieg closely trailed Harris with 16 percent support and Ocasio-Cortez tied Newsom at 14 percent. 

On the GOP side, Vice President JD Vance received 44 percent support for the Republican nomination and Secretary of State Marco Rubio received 21 percent.
news.summary: California governor’s name has been thrown out as a potential Democratic candidate in the 2028 presidential election — as have AOC, Pete Buttigieg and Kamala Harris
news.author: Rachel Dobkin

news.title: Stephen Colbert gets last laugh with ‘Late Show’ Emmy win after Trump attacks
news.text:
Stephen Colbert got the last laugh at the Emmys with a golden awards sendoff.

The former “Late Show” host victoriously took the stage Sept. 14 during the 78th Emmy Awards after his now-canceled late night CBS show won outstanding variety series, using the victory to advocate for his writing staff.

After pointing out that "if you like the comedy tonight, my old writers wrote it," Colbert said late-night shows are a "fantastic incubator for young people to come in" and learn how to work on a deadline.

"That is the future of our business that we have to look after," he said, adding that he has "great news" for the industry: His writers are now available to work. "Hire them. They will make your show better, and they will make your day easier."

Colbert also thanked those in the room who he has interviewed on his show but said his "favorite guest" is his wife, Evelyn McGee Colbert, whom he called the "only audience I really care about." 

The comedian also thanked her for being his "only audience" when he was taping his show at home during the COVID-19 pandemic.

"Yours is the laugh that I want for the rest of my life," he said. "I love you."

Colbert concluded his speech by thanking his viewers: "Thank you so much for watching. We hope you enjoyed the show. We had a great time doing it for you. That's it. Thank you. We'll catch you all on the flip."

The win capped a fitting Emmy farewell for Colbert and “The Late Show,” which ended its 11-season run at New York City's famed Ed Sullivan Theater in May after CBS announced it was pulling the plug on the late-night institution in July 2025.

Vote: Who had the best look at the Emmys? Vote for your favorites in USA TODAY's Emmys Style Meter.

The cancellation turned into an instant political flashpoint. CBS maintained the decision was a financial reality in the changing late-night landscape. But it came amid intense scrutiny over parent company Paramount's relationship with President Donald Trump. 

Paramount had agreed to a $16 million settlement of Trump's lawsuit over a CBS “60 Minutes” interview with Kamala Harris, a deal Colbert blasted on his show as a “big fat bribe.”

Trump publicly celebrated news of Colbert's cancellation.

"I absolutely love that Colbert got fired. His talent was even less than his ratings," Trump wrote in a July 18 Truth Social post, before also ripping ABC's Jimmy Kimmel, another late-night host known to poke fun at Trump. "I hear Jimmy Kimmel is next. Has even less talent than Colbert."

Colbert, one of TV's most artful Trump critics, continued hammering the president through his final months on the air.

One hour after the May 21 TV conclusion of the his late-night series – at 1:52 a.m. – Trump poured water on the jubilant show finale from his Truth Social account. "Colbert is finally finished at CBS. Amazing that he lasted so long! No talent, no ratings, no life." 

But Colbert opted not to get political during his Emmys speech, ignoring Trump entirely in his remarks.

This was Colbert's second consecutive Emmy win for "The Late Show": In his 2025 acceptance speech, he thanked CBS for "giving us the privilege to be part of the late-night tradition, which I hope continues long after we're no longer doing this show."

“The Late Show” entered the Sept. 14 Emmys ceremony with considerable momentum after winning five Creative Arts Emmys the previous weekend, including awards for writing and directing. 

Colbert actually endorsed "Jimmy Kimmel Live" competitor Jimmy Kimmel to win the category in a sincere Instagram post on the last day of Emmy voting.

The win comes the same week that Page Six reported on Sept. 8 that this season Kimmel's late-night show will be its last. ABC denied the report, calling it "inaccurate" and saying that "any reports about the future of the show at this point are purely speculative." Days later, USA TODAY learned that Kimmel and ABC are currently in talks to renew his long-running show.

Contributing: Brendan Morrow, USA TODAY

news.title: Newsom vs. Harris Chances Against Vance as Governor Defers to Former VP
news.text: California Governor Gavin Newsom said he would not run for president in 2028 if former Vice President Kamala Harris enters the race, as recent polling has shown both Democrats in close hypothetical matchups against Vice President JD Vance. “I wouldn’t run if she ran,” Newsom told CNN’s Jake Tapper in an interview that aired Monday. “Of course not, why would I? I wouldn’t do that to her. I wouldn’t do that to you. I wouldn’t waste everyone’s time. Who needs that?” he said. Recent Emerson College polling found Harris leading Vance 49 percent to 45 percent and Newsom leading him 49 percent to 44 percent in hypothetical 2028 matchups. Neither Harris nor Newsom has formally announced a 2028 presidential campaign, though both have signaled that they are considering a run. Vance has likewise not announced a campaign, but speculation about his 2028 prospects was on display at the Republican National Committee’s midterm convention in Dallas last week, where supporters chanted “48” during his keynote address. Newsom Says Primary Fight Against Harris Unserving Newsom said he believed a primary fight against Harris would serve little purpose, arguing that their overlapping Democratic constituencies would make the contest unnecessarily divisive. “First of all, electorally, it’s a gift from God for everybody else,” Newsom said. “It services no greater good.” Tapper pointed out that Harris has already had two chances to run for president, while Newsom has never launched a presidential campaign. “That would be the approach to the campaign, certainly,” Newsom said. “That would be the case you'd make, a pretty good one actually. That's objectively true.” Newsweek reached out to Harris and Newsom for comment. Newsom Says He Wasn't Ready in 2024 Newsom has previously faced questions about why he did not seek the Democratic nomination in 2024, when President Joe Biden was seeking reelection. He said he did not believe he had a sufficiently compelling reason to run at the time. “I wasn’t ready,” Newsom said. “No, God, no.” He said he would not have challenged Biden and questioned what his own rationale for running would have been. “I would have gotten crushed because I didn’t have a why,” Newsom said. “If you don’t have a big enough why, then you don’t belong there.” Newsom also said his four children would have to be on board with a presidential campaign and a candidate must be prepared to “meet the moment.” Early Polling Shows Close 2028 Matchups Early national polling has produced competitive hypothetical matchups between Newsom, Harris and Vance, although results vary by poll and the 2028 election remains years away. The latest national general-election poll listed by RealClearPolling was conducted by Emerson in August. It showed Newsom with 49 percent compared with 44 percent for Vance in a hypothetical matchup. The same poll showed Harris with 49 percent and Vance with 45 percent. Emerson’s survey was conducted August 16-17 among 1,000 likely voters. RealClearPolling also lists a September 5 Yahoo News poll in which Newsom received 49 percent compared with 41 percent for Vance. An earlier Zogby Analytics poll conducted January 1-7 among 891 likely voters found Harris ahead of Vance, 48.5 percent to 42.1 percent, with 9.4 percent saying they were not sure. In a hypothetical matchup between Newsom and Vance, however, the poll found Vance at 44.6 percent and Newsom at 41 percent, with 14.3 percent not sure. The poll had a margin of error of 3.3 percentage points. The Zogby poll also tested other potential 2028 matchups. Newsom led then-Secretary of State Marco Rubio 41.7 percent to 39.9 percent, with 18.4 percent not sure. Harris led Rubio 43.4 percent to 43.1 percent, with 13.5 percent not sure. Harris Leads Newsom in Early Democratic Polling While Newsom has been among the candidates tested in early Democratic primary polling, recent national surveys have generally placed Harris ahead of him. A Financial Times poll released September 6 showed Harris at 29 percent among potential Democratic primary voters, followed by Newsom at 14 percent. Pete Buttigieg was at 9 percent, while Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez was at 11 percent. A Harvard-Harris poll released September 2 showed Harris at 42 percent and Newsom at 18 percent. A Morning Consult poll released August 31 put Harris at 24 percent and Newsom at 12 percent. RealClearPolling's current national Democratic primary average puts Harris at 24.5 percent and Newsom at 13.5 percent, with other candidates also receiving support. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Newsom said he would not run for president in 2028 if Harris enters the race.
news.author: Alex Backus

news.title: Newsom says he won't run for president if Kamala Harris runs in 2028
news.text:
Stevensville, Montana -- We stood waist-deep in a cold Montana river, cursing at the elusive trout, and talking about whether he was going to run for president.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom had invited me and my crew to his in-laws' spread on Bitterroot Springs Ranch in Big Sky Country. I had pitched an idea to him, one I've been eager to experiment with for some time: a longform interview, not tied to news of the day, talking to people about their childhoods, their parents, some of their tougher moments and biggest successes of their lives.

I didn't want to do the interview in a chair, or a studio, or with makeup, or ties. I wanted to go where the interviewee felt comfortable. In addition to Newsom, a Democrat, I pitched the idea to a few others including Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio. Republican Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina has agreed to participate.

My horrible fly-fishing form notwithstanding, our fishing trek proved fruitful - if not for fish (though we caught a couple) - for conversation. Spending hours with someone driving around a ranch and standing in the frigid Bitterroot River has a way of loosening up even the most polished politician.

RELATED: Democratic CA Governor Gavin Newsom says he'll consider presidential run after 2026 midterms

Top of mind for Newsom is whether he runs for president in 2028. One of the key parts of that is who else is running, including his fellow San Francisco Democrat, former Vice President Kamala Harris.

"I don't know if she runs, but we'll see," Newsom told me. "I wouldn't run if she ran."

Frankly, I was stunned to hear that.

"Why would I?" he said. "I wouldn't do that to her. I wouldn't do it to me. ... I won't waste everyone's time. Who needs that?"

It didn't make sense to me.

"First of all, electorally it's a gift from God for everybody else," he explained. "They'd enjoy the hell out of it. Mutual assured destruction. It serves no greater good. Why would I do this if I wasn't trying to serve some greater good? There would be no upside whatsoever."

But what of the counterargument that she ran in 2019 and didn't even make it to 2020, then she ran again in 2024 and lost, I asked him.

"That would be the case you'd make," he acknowledged. "Pretty good one, actually. That's objectively true. But I know what that means. I know her base of supporters, I know her friends, the (Venn) diagram on that is just pure crossover ... I wouldn't do that to people. I wouldn't put them in that position ... Every other Democrat is praying for that, and every other Republican is gonna pray for that. And that's just not gonna happen."

How do you even decide if you're going to run for president?

"I have no experience in this process, so I'm going through it," Newsom said. I noted some folks wished he had challenged President Joe Biden in 2024.

MORE: California Gov. Gavin Newsom says Department of Justice is investigating him and his wife

"I wasn't ready," he said. "First of all, I wouldn't do that. And second, if I did, I would have gotten crushed because I didn't have a why. You don't have big enough why, then you don't belong there."

"It's shocking how many presidential candidates can't answer their why. Like, shocking," he continued. He said he'd seen "leading candidates over the last few cycles that are there for the wrong reasons. Or no reason at all, which is the worst. So, you've got to have a big enough why."

After decades in public life - and we talked about it all, his dyslexia, his failed first marriage, his ignominious affair with the wife of a mayoral aide, his mother's assisted suicide, a close friend telling him he needed to get his shit together, his governor's race, the challenges of Covid-19, his confrontations with President Donald Trump, and much more - he said, "I am not screwing anything up anymore, man. I know what matters in life. I got four kids, it's the only thing that matters to me."

His wife and school-aged children, he said, would have to agree to a White House run. "If they're not on board, that's a non-starter."

In the flowing water, Newsom checked his hook and then cast his line again, looking upstream at the signs of the fish refusing to bite and telling me the signs that might make him run.

"You just have to meet the moment. You got to be honest with yourself. Do you represent the zeitgeist in the moment, or are you wasting everybody's time?" he said.

"I'm not here to make a point. I want to make the difference, and you can make a difference in a lot of ways in life."

news.title: Newsom says he won't run for president if Harris does
news.text: Gov. Gavin Newsom said he would not run for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2028 if Kamala Harris does so, appearing to offer deference to the former vice president ahead of a race that could draw a historically crowded field of candidates. "I wouldn't run if she ran," Newsom told CNN's Jake Tapper in an interview posted Monday. "Why would I? I wouldn't do that to her. ... I wouldn't do it to you, I wouldn't waste everyone's time." Newsom appeared to acknowledge a desire to avoid the possibly messy fight for California backers that could ensue if both were to run, saying there would be "pure crossover" between Harris' supporters and his. The governor's effective yield to Harris diminishes the possibility of a showdown between two of California's most powerful political figures in an election whose stakes are viewed by the Democratic Party as existential. The possibility of Harris making a second attempt at the presidency after her loss to President Trump in 2024 has hung as the biggest question over the potential Democratic field. Both Newsom and Harris have acknowledged they are considering presidential bids in 2028, but Harris has closely held her intentions. She said last week that she had not decided whether to run, telling former soccer player Megan Rapinoe in a podcast interview that she was focused on working full time to help Democrats win the midterms. A spokesperson for Harris declined to comment. Representatives for Newsom did not immediately respond to a request Monday afternoon. Harris has appeared as the party front-runner in multiple polls about 2028, including one in July that showed her beating Newsom by double digits. But questions have continually circulated within the party about whether voters who are scarred from the party's 2024 loss would be enthusiastic about a Harris run. Several California donors told The Times in May that they did not plan to support Harris or did not want to discuss a possible bid by her; in a few corners, more enthusiasm came through for Newsom. The dynamics around the 2028 Democratic primary continue to evolve as party hopefuls jockey for the spotlight, and they shifted notably with the selection of South Carolina as the party's first primary state. That choice could give Harris a boost if South Carolina's Black voters move in her favor. Harris and Newsom came up in politics in the same era and have never before run in an election against each other, operating their political careers largely in parallel rather than in competition. In February, Newsom said on CNN that he had "never gotten in the way of her ambition" and he didn't "imagine I would in the future," saying "fate" would determine whether they ran against each other. Newsom swung through South Carolina this month, the type of move generally interpreted as laying the groundwork for a presidential bid. In the CNN interview, Newsom noted that he did not know whether Harris would run and agreed it was a "pretty good case" to make when Tapper raised the argument that Harris had had her chance at the presidency and Newsom had not yet. The governor suggested that a fight between him and Harris would split their supporters' vote in a way that would be "a gift from God for everybody else" in the race, saying "it services no greater good" for both of them to run. He also nodded to their overlapping political circles. "I know her base of supporters, I know her friends. The [Venn] diagram on that is just pure crossover," Newsom said. "I wouldn't do that." The interview was filmed in Montana, where Newsom’s in-laws own a ranch, as Newsom and Tapper fly-fished together. The full segment was set to air Tuesday. Newsom said that in order to decide to run, a candidate needs to be able to "meet the moment." "You gotta be honest with yourself," he said. "Do you represent the zeitgeist of the moment or are you wasting everybody's time?"
news.summary: Newsom's effective yield to Harris diminishes the possibility of a 2028 showdown between two of California's most powerful political figures.
news.author: Justine McDaniel

news.title: Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed says leaders must address ‘unpaid debts’ to Black communities
news.text: Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed said Saturday that the country must confront what he described as "unpaid debts" owed to Black communities, arguing that leaders have a responsibility to "understand" and "address" them. El-Sayed — who is facing Republican nominee and former Rep. Mike Rogers in one of the nation's most closely watched Senate races — made the remarks while speaking at a meeting with women faith leaders hosted by the Woman Difference Collaborative in Detroit, according to a video shared by C-SPAN. "When it comes to black communities in Michigan — when it comes to black communities in America — there are unpaid debts that have long since come due that we are unwilling to acknowledge, let alone pay down," El-Sayed said. "And I understand that we need leaders who are going to understand those debts and address them." ABDUL EL-SAYED PROTESTED AGAINST 'EX-TERRORISTS' WHO CONVERTED TO CHRISTIANITY, UNEARTHED REPORT REVEALS El-Sayed made the remarks while responding to a question about how he plans to energize Democratic voters who did not support him in the primary. He said his approach is to keep showing up, engaging with voters and emphasizing his record. "But the question for me is, within my power have I done my best?" El-Sayed said. "And I will challenge people to look at my history and say, ‘Yeah, that man hasn’t done everything he could around the problems he says he cares about.'" ABDUL EL-SAYED DISMISSES QUESTIONS ABOUT HASAN PIKER TIES ON 'FACE THE NATION,' PIVOTS TO GROCERIES During his response, El-Sayed highlighted his work on infant and maternal mortality, asthma and lead exposure. He also called for expanding access to capital for small businesses and increasing investment in housing and schools. El-Sayed, a former Wayne County health director, unsuccessfully ran for Michigan governor in 2018 before launching his Senate campaign. news.title: Ex-Dem insider exposes what Harris told top donors days before Biden dropped out: 'Insulting'
news.text: FIRST ON FOX: Lindy Li, a former Democratic fundraiser who switched party affiliation over unheeded warning signs about President Joe Biden's decline in the 2024 election, believes Kamala Harris was setting herself up to poach Biden’s donors just days before he dropped out of the race — while still telling voters he could win. Li said she threaded that political needle by staying far away from any criticism of Biden. "It was all charade. She was auditioning for Biden's endorsement, and the way that she did it was by imposing a fake rule on her staff to not talk about her ascending to the nomination," Li said in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital. Li’s chronicling of the months leading up to Biden's suspended campaign, which are included in her book, "Unburdened," adds more detail about how even those closest to Biden understood that his campaign would likely come to a grinding halt following his disastrous 2024 debate — and even before it. EX-BIDEN STAFFER BLAMES BIDEN'S 'HUBRIS' FOR THE 'HELLSCAPE THAT WE LIVE IN': REPORT As a top fundraiser for both Biden and Harris and someone who had achieved a high profile with the Democratic National Committee (DNC), Li worked with both teams to raise campaign contributions. In the wake of the election, Li has gone public with much of her insider knowledge, raising the alarm over just how many figures inside the Democratic Party had seen the writing on the wall but remained silent. She also detailed how others, like Harris, quickly moved to prepare themselves for what would happen next. In Li’s view, Harris prioritized face time with donors she knew could soon back her own bid. "I was on the call; she would host calls with donors and pretend to support Biden and say there's no daylight between Biden and herself. All the while she was auditioning for those very donors," Li said. HARRIS REACHES OUT TO SOCIALIST MAYOR MAMDANI IN LATEST SIGN SHE'S SHORING UP SUPPORT FOR POSSIBLE 2028 BID Li recalled how, in one case, Harris addressed donors about Biden’s viability as a candidate two days before Biden bowed out. "It was either on July 19th or July 20th. Actually, I think it was July 19, 2024; Kamala Harris held a call saying that there was no way that Biden would drop out and that she would stick with him until the end. And these were some of the biggest donors in the party," Li recalled. Biden announced that he would no longer pursue reelection on July 21. After Biden’s announcement, Li recalled that Harris moved aggressively within the Democratic camp to shore up support, insinuating that she had some form of Biden’s backing. "She was flattering people left and right. The first 24 hours were a very intensive charm offensive on her part. And that's how she was able to consolidate it so quickly. She flattered people up the wazoo. It made it abundantly clear that Biden had endorsed her. And Biden initially — I don't know if people know this, but he didn't want to endorse her right away. news.title: Jon Ossoff vs. Mike Collins: New GOP Poll Gives Race Update 50 Days Out
news.text: Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff led Republican Representative Mike Collins by more than six points in a new survey from pollster Trafalgar Group. The poll was published this weekend, just before the 50-day mark ahead of the November 3 midterms. The poll is the latest in a series of polls showing Ossoff with a lead in the Peach State, as the Georgia Senate race remains one of the most closely watched contests of the midterms. Republicans believe the race is competitive, pointing to President Donald Trump’s 2-point victory over former Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024. But Democrats believe that Trump’s national approval rating, which has declined amid economic concerns, could give them an advantage in the closely divided swing state. Although Georgia backed Trump in 2024, former President Joe Biden won it four years earlier in 2020, and it reelected Democratic Senator Raphael Warnock in 2022. Growth around the blue-shifting Atlanta metro has turned the once-Republican state into a battleground, and Democrats hope those trends will continue to boost Ossoff this year. Georgia Senate Poll Gives Jon Ossoff a Lead Ossoff received support from 49.4 percent of respondents, while Collins’ support stood at 42.8 percent, according to the poll. Only 1.3 percent said they would vote for Libertarian candidate Allen Buckley, while 6.5 percent were still undecided, the poll found. It surveyed 1,091 respondents from September 10-12 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 2.9 percentage points. Trafalgar was founded by Robert Cahaly, who has served as a political consultant for Republicans, and is generally seen as having a Republican lean. It has overestimated Republicans in some races, particularly in 2022, but also correctly predicted Trump’s victory in 2016 even as many other pollsters forecasted that former Secretary of State Hillary Clinton held an advantage. An Ossoff campaign spokesperson told Newsweek, “Georgia is a battleground state and Senator Ossoff is already facing millions of dollars of Republican spending against him. The Ossoff campaign will continue to build unstoppable momentum and work to earn every vote across the state of Georgia.” Newsweek also reached out to the Collins campaign for comment via email. What Other Polls Show Other recent polling similarly gives Ossoff a lead over Collins, who was first elected to the House of Representatives in 2022. Ossoff led by 7 points in the latest poll from InsiderAdvantage, which placed the Democratic incumbent’s support at 50 percent, while 43 percent said they would vote for Collins. Seven percent of respondents said they were undecided about how they would vote in the general election. The poll surveyed 800 likely voters August 16 to 17 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.46 percentage points. It was first reported by James Magazine, a statewide political publication in Georgia. Collins trailed Ossoff by 9 points in a recent poll from AARP, 52 percent to 43 percent. It was conducted by Fabrizio Ward and Impact Research among 1,060 likely voters July 13-16, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. A recent Wick survey showed Ossoff up by 4 points with 46.7 percent to Collins’ 42.9 percent. It surveyed 1,175 likely voters from June 27-30, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.9 percentage points. Ossoff held a larger lead in an earlier Fox News poll of 13 points, 56 percent to 43 percent. It surveyed 1,002 registered voters from June 23 to 27, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. What Prediction Markets Show Ossoff is favored in prediction markets, holding a 94 percent chance of victory on Kalshi and a 93 percent in January. His chances on Kalshi have increased steadily throughout the election cycle. On Kalshi, Ossoff had a 91 percent chance of winning on August 1, an 85 percent chance of winning as of July 2, an 81 percent chance as of June 2 and a 75 percent chance of winning as of the start of the year on January 1. Prediction markets allow traders to buy and sell contracts tied to political outcomes and current events, aggregating real‑money wagers into probability estimates. Prices fluctuate as traders react to polling, fundraising, candidate developments and broader political trends. They measure trader sentiment at a given moment but do not always accurately predict the future. A New Battleground Georgia was once viewed as more reliably Republican during the 2000s and 2010s but has steadily shifted toward competitive status due to rapid growth and demographic change in Atlanta and its surrounding suburbs. In fact, some of Atlanta’s suburbs were among the only places in the country to get more Democratic from 2020 to 2024, despite major shifts rightward elsewhere across the nation—a sign of how quickly these areas are trending leftward. Democrats hope those trends accelerate in 2026 as they work to continue building progress in Georgia. Trump carried Georgia by about 2.2 points in the 2024 presidential election, after Joe Biden won the state by roughly 0.2 points in 2020. Trump won Georgia by about 5 points in 2016, while Mitt Romney won it by roughly 8 points in 2012 and John McCain by about 5 points in 2008. Jon Ossoff Calls for AI Action in Speech Over the weekend, a clip of Ossoff calling for action on artificial intelligence spread across social media. “Tech titans dig bunkers while warning us the new intelligence they're creating risks human extinction. Congress debates youth sports, and the president builds a ballroom. An ancient establishment, barely capable of email, sleepwalks into a technological revolution, while the president dismantles precautions and calls us fools for worrying,” he said. Ossoff said a “capable Congress” would engage every committee in investigation and legislation to “act swiftly and wisely,” but said Republicans “sit on their hands and hope for the best.” His comments came after Jacob Coxon, a former AI researcher for Anthropic and OpenAI, wrote in a post on X that he resigned from his role at Anthropic and warned that he believes AI could “kill us all by the end of the decade,” sparking greater calls for Congress to address regulation. Georgia Is Must-Win State Republicans currently have a 53-47 Senate majority, so Democrats must flip four seats to win control of the chamber but are facing a challenging map, as Vice President JD Vance would serve as the tiebreaker in an evenly divided Senate. Control of the Senate is seen as increasingly up for grabs ahead of November. Georgia is one of two Democratic-held seats in states Trump won in the 2024 election that is up for grabs in November—along with Michigan. Democrats view North Carolina, which Trump won by 3 points, and Maine, which he lost by 7 points, as their top flip opportunities in November. But no other GOP-held seats are up for grabs in states Trump won or lost by single digits, so Democrats have to turn to more conservative states to compete for Senate control. They view seats in states like Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas, all of which backed Trump by double digits in 2024, as their next best opportunities. Polls show close races in each of those states. Contact Newsweek editors for this story: Jason Lemon and Anthony Murray.

news.title: Newsom Says He Won't Run in 2028 if Kamala Harris Jumps In: 'Why Would I?'
news.text:
California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) told CNN he will not run for president in 2028 if former Vice President Kamala Harris enters the race.

Newsom made the comment during a fly-fishing outing in Montana with CNN’s Jake Tapper, as part of an ongoing series that was announced on Monday in which the anchor joins politicians in their favorite places to discuss their careers. Tapper pressed Newsom on the crowded Democrat field, noting he was not even the only potential candidate from California before naming Rep. Ro Khanna (D-CA) and Harris.

“I don’t know if she runs, but we’ll see,” Newsom said. When Tapper noted Harris had “called around,” the governor added, “But I wouldn’t run if she ran.”

Tapper asked him to confirm the line.

“Of course not. Why would I? I wouldn’t do that to her,” Newsom said. “I wouldn’t waste everyone’s time. Who needs that?”

Newsom argued a primary between the two Californians would only benefit the rest of the field, describing the scenario as “mutually assured destruction.”

“Electorally, it’s a gift from God for everybody else,” he said. “It services no greater good.”

WATCH — DJ Daniel: Kamala Harris, Gavin Newsom Are Democrats Who Do Nothing:

Tapper pushed back, pointing out that Harris has run for president twice while Newsom never has. The governor conceded the point but said their coalitions overlap too heavily.

“That would be the case you’d make. Pretty good one, actually,” Newsom said. “I know her base of supporters. I know her friends. The Venn diagram on that is just pure crossover.”

Newsom also said any decision would be run through his family first, calling his potential run for president a “non-starter” if he does not have the support of his four children.

The remarks come as Newsom trails Harris in early primary polling. A Harvard-Harris survey in April found 50 percent of Democrats preferred Harris as the 2028 nominee, compared to 22 percent for Newsom. Harris has said she “might” run again and told the BBC last year, “I am not done.” Neither has formally declared a candidacy.

news.title: New data shows voting differences within individual Asian American groups along gender lines, immigration timeframes
news.text:
By Carolyn Bick
NORTHWEST ASIAN WEEKLY

Migration trends, cultural memory, religious trends, and socioeconomic trends underpin many of the decisions Asian Americans make—including when it comes to voting. Data collected by nonpartisan research organization NORC at the University of Chicago, in partnership with the Committee of 100, even shows distinct differences within individual Asian American communities, both generationally and between women and men, as well as shifts in political leanings over time.

Between 2020 and 2024, Asian Americans recorded the largest increase in eligible voters compared with other racial and ethnic groups, said Nathan Chan, an assistant professor of political science at Loyola Marymount University. As of 2026, there are 16 million eligible AAPI voters, 1.6 million of whom are newly eligible as of 2022. Voter turnout among both Asian Americans and Pacific Islanders has significantly increased since 2014.

These findings underscore this fact, and show that politicians must better acknowledge and engage Asian American voters, as they consider future campaigns.

“A community this large, this fast-growing, could increasingly determine election outcomes,” Chan said. “Nearly one in five [Asian Americans] identify as non-partisan, which is a reminder that this electorate’s vote should not be taken for granted.”

Chan participated in a Committee of 100 panel to unpack the findings with APIA Vote’s co-founder and moderator, Scott Wang, senior congressional reporter at NBC News. NORC collected the data as part of its Amplify AAPI and AmeriSpeak panels last June. The panels surveyed 1,046 Asian Americans, 717 of whom identified as Chinese Americans. The Sept. 10 roundtable concluded a four-part series focusing on Chinese Americans in the run-up to this year’s midterm elections.

More Chinese American women, U.S.-born Chinese Americans vote Democrat

The data showed that even amongst Chinese Americans, who as a whole tend to vote Democrat, there are distinct voting differences.

Notably, Chinese American women were more likely to vote Democrat than Chinese American men by a wide margin—64% to 44%. This is a larger gender gap than within in Black, Latino, or white populations.

Chan said that it wasn’t so much the difference itself—generally speaking, women tend to lean Democrat, while men tend to lean Republican—as it was the magnitude of difference between Chinese American women and men that was so striking.

“We should be cautious about saying exactly why this might be the case on the data alone. However, one possibility is that some of the issues that are producing gender differences in the electorate, such as our discussions about abortion, reproductive rights, social safety nets, are really resonating with Chinese American women particularly. And Chinese American women are really perceiving, I think, certain political parties as more friendly on issues of gender and diversity.”

Chinese American men also leaned considerably more Republican, and U.S.-born Chinese Americans are more likely to vote Democrat than their Chinese-born peers.

Timing of immigration also affects party affiliation, the studies found. Chinese Americans who immigrated to the United States before 1980 tended to vote Democrat more often than those who immigrated here after 2010.

Asian Americans unafraid to cross party lines

In the 2024 election, 64% of Chinese Americans voted for Kamala Harris, while 31% voted for Trump. This was consistent with Latino voters, researchers found.

But compared with Republicans in the rest of the voting public, Chinese American and Asian American Republicans appeared to be the most willing to cross party lines in the 2024 presidential election to vote for Harris.

“A fair share of Chinese American Republicans did cross party lines. Eleven percent of Chinese American Republicans voted for the Democratic presidential candidate, Kamala Harris,” Chan said. “Among Asian American Republicans more broadly, that willingness to cross over actually reached 20%, surpassing the rate of cross-party voting seen among Republican voters of other racial and ethnic backgrounds.”

This trend also continued down-ballot in state and other national races. Between 16%-17% of Chinese American Republicans voted for a Democrat in House, Senate, or gubernatorial races in 2024. Amongst Asian American Republicans, 13% voted for a Democratic House candidate, while 17% voted for both a Democratic Senate and gubernatorial candidate.

Continued lack of outreach to growing AAPI electorate

The survey data also showed that both parties continue to fail to conduct much, if any, outreach amongst Asian American voters. Among those surveyed, 42% of Asian Americans reported no contact from the Democratic Party, and 58% reported no contact from the Republican Party.

Chen said that for the last 15 years, both parties have done a better job of investing in the Asian American electorate, and that each party started doing this at different times. For instance, she said, the Democratic National Committee has hired an AAPI person to do outreach since 2008. The Republican National Committee “decided to finally invest dollars in investing in ethnic press and some type of communication strategy to reach Asian American voters” in 2013 or 2014.

“But it’s still very inconsistent. When you look at campaigns and political parties, they tend to focus on just high propensity voters,” or voters who are registered and vote every single election cycle, Chen said. “So they don’t have to really do a lot of heavy convincing of getting you to turn out to vote. They’re just going to focus on why you should vote for their particular candidate.”

But this ignores the “reality” of the growth of the Asian American and Pacific Islander electorate, she said.

“We have many first-time voters, whether they’re aging in, naturalizing, and also a large base who finally understand the importance of the vote, especially as related to representation and addressing issues that they care about,” Chen said. So, she continued, from her point of view, neither the Democratic nor the Republican Party is keeping up with the growth of the electorate, and the investments the parties are making in the electorate are still “uneven, in terms of the investments that they put in during a presidential election cycle versus in midterm elections.”

She also noted that part of the issue surrounding voting for the AAPI community is “the broader challenge of trying to convince these political parties that they also need to be engaging the space of voters outside of the elections. It really should be engaging them and bringing them in to actually showing up at their events, talking to them, addressing their particular issues.”

Political, religious histories influence voting

However, as a whole, Chinese Americans, Vietnamese Americans, and Filipino Americans showed higher rates of support for President Donald Trump than Japanese Americans or Korean Americans.

But again, the information alone doesn’t tell the whole story. It doesn’t give a sense of why this is. For instance, Chan said, Vietnamese Americans’ migration history is inextricably connected to issues related to geopolitics and communism, which has led especially older generations of Vietnamese Americans to tend to vote Republican.

Similarly, Filipino Americans “have a really distinctive religious profile compared to many other Asian American groups,” with large Catholic and Christian populations. This religious leaning, Chan said, “can lead some Filipino American Republicans to support Trump a little bit more.”

While Filipino Americans appear to continue to be voting more conservatively, Chen said, this doesn’t mean that communities simply stay the same. For instance, she said, the tide appears to be shifting amongst Vietnamese Americans, as the community grows. “They started out as being a lot more conservative, but in more recent survey data, we’re showing that a number of them tend to be more moderate or progressive.”

Information sourcing plays key role

Chen also highlighted that where communities get their information from is also important, and that has to do with both time of arrival and English proficiency. This, in turn, appears to influence voting trends.

“We know that Indian Americans and Japanese Americans tend to be a lot more progressive or democratic leaning—but they also are more English proficient,” she said. “They’re going to rely on English language news, versus when you look at Chinese, Korean, and Vietnamese, there’s gonna be a lot more limited English proficient communities.”

“And so where are they getting their information from?” she continued. “Are they also in chat rooms with other aunties and uncles? When they’re introducing information and links, where is that coming from, or is that coming from abroad?”

Chen appealed to listeners to help educate their families and friends who may be struggling with overwhelming and outright misinformation regarding the upcoming midterms. This includes important information about whether they can use mail-in ballots and when those ballots are due. Chen said that it’s important to help them make a plan to vote.

“Their trusted messengers are really their family and friends. According to our survey, it’s also journalists and academics,” she said. “Everyone is exhausted, but they’re going to turn to their family and friends.”
news.summary: Migration trends, cultural memory, religious trends, and socioeconomic trends underpin many of the decisions Asian Americans make—including when it comes to voting.

news.title: Gavin Newsom — While Fishing With Jake Tapper — Says He’s Out on 2028 Run if Kamala Harris Is In
news.text:
If she’s in, he’s out.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom (D) told CNN anchor Jake Tapper he will not run for president in 2028 if former Vice President Kamala Harris decides to try again. The liberal governor dished the revelation on Monday while he and Tapper were recorded fly fishing together in Montana — and it appeared to mildly stun the news host.

“I wouldn’t run if she ran,” Newsom said.

Tapper turned to the gov while holding his poll in the air and confirmed, “If she runs, you will not?”

Newsom acted like it was obvious he should bow out if Harris opts to run.

“Of course not, why would I?” he answered. “I wouldn’t do that to her, I wouldn’t do that to you, I wouldn’t waste everyone’s time. Who needs that?”

His answer baffled Tapper.

“What do you mean?” the host asked. “That doesn’t even make sense.”

“No, I wouldn’t,” Newsom continued. “First of all, electorally, it’s a gift from God for everybody else that can enjoy the hell out of it. Mutuality assured destruction, it services no greater good.”

The two guys — who were both sporting sunglasses and baseball caps while standing side-by-side in a stream — kept casting as they weighed the ’28 race.

Tapper told Newsom, “You do whatever you want, I don’t care” — which drew a laugh from the governor — before making the case why he should run.

“My counterargument would be like, she had a shot, and you’ve never run, and she’s run twice,” Tapper explained.

Newsom said it was “objectively true” and would be a pretty good case for him to make on the campaign trail — but he still wasn’t interested. He said the Venn diagram — which sounded like he mispronounced and called a “Zen Diagram” — between him and Harris supporters was “pure crossover,” so it didn’t make sense to run.

The governor’s announcement stands out, considering most betting markets give him the better odds of being the Democratic nominee than Harris. Newsom has the third-best chance — behind Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-GA) and Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-NY) — of being the Democratic nominee on both Polymarket and Kalshi, which give him a 13% shot. Harris, for comparison, is being given an 8% chance on both.

The full Tapper-Newsom fishing interview is slated to run on Tuesday.

news.title: James Talarico Can't Possibly Be Winning Texas
news.text:
This time the great hope is Texas State Rep. James Talarico (D-50th District), and several recent polls show him ahead in his Senate race, enough to rattle some Republicans. But before anyone declares Texas is gonna flip, it's worth asking a simple question: does anyone seriously think James Talarico is the guy who finally pulls this off?

The last Democrat to win a Texas Senate race was Lloyd Bentsen, in 1988. Texas hasn't elected a Democrat to statewide office since 1994. Donald Trump carried the state by 14 points in 2024. It is exceedingly rare for a state that hands a president a double-digit win to flip to the opposing party's non-incumbent candidate two years later.

Republican Ken Paxton, the state attorney general, has already won statewide office in Texas. Do I think a moderate Democrat could conceivably beat him under the right conditions? It’s not out of the realm of possibility. There have been signs that Texas was trending purple, but after Trump won Texas by 14 points, I just don’t see that happening. And even if it were possible, Talarico is not that Democrat. To win statewide, he needs voters who backed Trump to cross over for him, and it's fair to ask what, exactly, is supposed to make that happen.

ICYMI: Ken Paxton Absolutely Schooled James Talarico, and It Was Brutal

His positions on religion, transgenderism, and women's sports sit far outside the mainstream in a Republican-leaning state. Heck, I would argue that they’re too radical for the voters of a blue state.

And make no mistake about it, we know his record. Talarico has said "God is non-binary" and claimed there are "six genders.” His professed love of "trans" children is extremely creepy, and now, newly resurfaced remarks add yet another troubling piece to the puzzle that is James Talarico.

Back in 2019, Talarico argued during a Texas Legislature committee hearing that parents denying their child’s gender identity was essentially child abuse.

"I think there are some folks that would think that if you deny your child's gender identity, that's incredibly harmful," he said. "And whether or not we label it with the term abuse, it's abusive for sure."

His remarks came during debate over HB 1910, a bill that would have barred courts from treating a parent's refusal to affirm a child's gender identity as evidence of unfitness in custody disputes. The bill's text stated that courts "may not consider evidence regarding whether the party demonstrates a history or pattern of acknowledging or declining to acknowledge the child's gender identity or expression" when deciding custody. Talarico opposed it, arguing that ruling out any link to abuse "is dangerous and could certainly harm some of our most vulnerable kids in the state."

He went further. "Some of us I think really do consider this abusive behavior… an unwillingness to identify, acknowledge a child's gender identity," Talarico said. "We consider that abusive to the child, abusive and destructive."

This is not an abstract concept Talarico is pushing, either. In Massachusetts, a family is fighting to regain custody of their teenage daughter and stop the state from medically transitioning her with high-dose testosterone. Sophie was 15 when the Massachusetts Department of Children and Families removed her from her parents' home in December of 2024. A counselor at her school reportedly socially transitioned her to a male identity without their knowledge or consent.

Do you think a majority of Texas voters would condone that by voting for Talarico?

Heck, Talarico doesn’t even believe it. He is now working overtime to convince voters his well-documented fascination with trans ideology doesn't reflect who he really is today. If you wanted a sign that his internal polling numbers aren't as rosy as the public polls suggest, there it is.

I’m not trying to be that guy who argues every poll that he doesn’t like is fake, but when a poll showed Kamala Harris a mere five points behind Trump in 2024, I knew better than to believe it.

news.title: AOC and Ro Khanna 2028? What Polls Show Amid Progressive Push for Campaign
news.text: Progressive organizations are calling on Representatives Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York and Ro Khanna to run in the 2028 Democratic presidential primary. The groups RootsAction and Progressive Democrats of America announced a new campaign urging the two progressive lawmakers to run for president after the 2026 midterm elections. Progressive Democrats of America notably launched the “Run, Bernie, Run” campaign back in 2013, ahead of Vermont Senator Bernie Sanders’ 2016 presidential run, which was seen as a pivotal point in the progressive movement. The groups wrote that it is “crucial” for progressives to be at the top of the ticket, in a joint statement published on Monday. “Without a progressive populist advocate atop the ticket, the Democratic response would be woefully underwhelming — enabling right-wing demagoguery to push voter unrest in dangerous and divisive directions,” the groups wrote. They said they did not give either lawmaker advance knowledge of the campaign but that they “definitely want to see one or both of them in the race.” Newsweek reached out to spokespersons for Ocasio-Cortez and Khanna for comment via email. AOC and Ro Khanna’s Chances in the Polls Typically, candidates do not start announcing presidential runs until after the midterms, but potential candidates are already traveling to key primary states to build up their name recognition, test their message and make inroads with voters who may be decisive in how the 2028 contest plays out. Early polls are not always predictive of final outcomes, but they do have major implications for candidates. Donors and voters use polls to gauge whether a candidate is viable, so the numbers matter to a candidate's ability to fundraise and garner media attention. They also measure initial name recognition among potential candidates. Most recent polls show former Vice President Kamala Harris, who is already well known among Democrats, with an early lead among primary voters. Other top contenders include California Governor Gavin Newsom, former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, Georgia Senator Jon Ossoff, Arizona Senator Mark Kelly and Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro. Ocasio-Cortez received 11 percent, while Khanna polled at 1 percent in the latest survey from Echelon Insights. It found Harris in the lead with 18 percent, followed by Buttigieg and Newsom at 13 percent and 12 percent, respectively. It surveyed 1,002 likely voters from August 13 to 17, 2026, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.4 percentage points. Meanwhile, a FocalData poll showed Ocasio-Cortez with 10 percent and Khanna with 1 percent. Harris also led that poll with 31 percent support, while Newsom placed second with 13 percent. It surveyed 2,178 adults from August 28 to September 2, 2026. What Have AOC and Ro Khanna Said About 2028? Ocasio-Cortez addressed presidential speculation in May in a conversation with David Axelrod, who served as an adviser to former President Barack Obama. "My ambition is to change this country,” she said. “Presidents come and go. Senate, House seats, elected officials come and go. But single-payer healthcare is forever. A living wage is forever, workers' rights are forever, women's rights, all of that, and so anyways...to a finer point to your question is that when you aren't attached, when you haven't been like fantasizing about being this or that since the time you were 7 years old, it is tremendously liberating." Khanna has said he is “thinking seriously” about running in 2028, telling NPR in August that the country could “break” if it does not “do something dramatically different.” I'm the nice guy. I just want a new social contract. Have you met these folks in their 30s? They want pitchforks and torches. They want your scalps… politically,” he told NPR. He said Ocasio-Cortez’s decision would have “no bearing” on his own choice. “I have a vision called economic patriotism, which calls for having the greatest economic mission in generations to build a future economy that's going to be working for people I grew up with, deindustrialized communities, the black South. How do we bring economic success, not just in Silicon Valley, across this country?” he said. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Jason Lemon and Gray R. Thomas
news.summary: Progressive groups are pressing Ocasio-Cortez and Khanna to run for president in 2028.

news.title: 'You’ve Got to Show Up': WNBA Executives Blast Cathy Engelbert’s Absence at Caitlin Clark’s Home Games Ahead of Leadership Change
news.text:
Cathy Engelbert’s decision to retire after seven years as WNBA commissioner comes at a moment when league insiders are openly questioning her leadership. Days after her announcement, executives voiced frustration over her absence from key moments, especially Caitlin Clark’s home games in Indiana.

“These jobs, you have to go in with your eyes open because that is the job,” said one executive, per Tom Friend of Sports Business Journal. “It’s not dropping in, et cetera. You’ve got to show up. It’s every weekend. … You just have to be there.”

Over the past two seasons, that criticism has become the league’s open secret. Engelbert rarely appeared at public events or during controversies, leaving players and executives feeling abandoned. Her absence isolated her from the league’s power centers, a fatal misstep for any commissioner.

According to SBJ’s Tom Friend, Engelbert never attended an Indiana Fever home game since Clark joined the league in 2024. For a commissioner to lack relationships with general managers, coaches, or star players like Clark undermines trust and credibility. 

Napheesa Collier underscored that point in her fiery exit interview last year, saying Engelbert told her Clark should be “grateful” for the platform the WNBA provided.

The perception of disengagement deepened after the Alyssa Thomas-Caitlin Clark incident, when Thomas pressed her fist to Clark’s throat. The controversy spread like wildfire, drawing a letter from Republican lawmakers demanding accountability. 

Thomas later revealed she faced harassment and death threats, yet Engelbert never publicly stepped up. “Here we are with all this stuff that’s happened,” one team executive told ESPN. “And it just, at different points, has felt like, ‘Where are you?’”

For stakeholders, Engelbert’s absence carried bigger repercussions. Conversations with more than 20 insiders, including owners, management, and players, revealed a consensus: while Engelbert oversaw business growth, she wasn’t the right person to navigate the league’s current demands.

As NBA Commissioner Adam Silver and WNBA ownership begin the search for her successor, executives say they want “someone who can work a locker room and a corporate room, someone who can mesmerize the masses with a speech.” 

Speculation has already centered on Michelle Obama and Kamala Harris as potential replacements, though the process will only begin once the 2026 season concludes.
news.summary: Cathy Engelbert’s decision to retire after seven years as WNBA commissioner comes at a moment when league insiders are openly questioning her leadership.

news.title: Musk PAC takes aim at Maine congressional races
news.text:
(The Center Square) — The world's “richest man” is pumping money into Maine's congressional races as part of broader efforts to keep control of Congress in Republican hands. 

Tesla CEO Elon Musk's America PAC has begun spending money to back GOP candidates in key battleground states ahead of November's pivotal midterm elections, starting with the closely watched race between incumbent Sen. Susan Collins and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson in Maine. 

To date, Musk's PAC has already spent $170,000 on digital ads, mailers, texts and phone calls in support of Collin's reelection bid, according to Federal Election Commission filings. 

Collins is facing a formidable challenge from Democrat Jackson, an Allagash logger and former state Senate President, who was recently chosen by the party to replace disgraced Senate candidate Graham Platner after he dropped out of the race in early July amid allegations of sexual assault.

The Maine race is considered a must-win contest for the Democratic Party as it pushes to retake the U.S. Senate, where Republicans currently have a 53-45 majority. Both parties are channeling tens of millions of dollars into a crush of TV and digital advertising to sway undecided voters ahead of the election.

Collins, a moderate who has been politically untouchable for the past three decades, is the only Republican senator running for reelection this year in a Democratic-led state that Kamala Harris carried in the 2024 presidential election.

The latest poll shows a competitive race with Jackson ahead of Collins by more than two percentage points, but within the margin of error.

The Senate Leadership Fund, a Republican super PAC, has committed more than $42 million to the Maine race. 

But Musk's post-primary season spending spree is also targeting Maine's wide open 2nd Congressional District race, where Trump-backed former Republican Gov. Paul LePage is facing Democratic State Auditor Matt Dunlap in fight to fill the seat vacated by outgoing Rep Jared Golden, a Democrat who isn't seeking reelection. 

Musk's PAC has contributed $21,000 to the congressional race to date, according to FEC disclosures, which has paid for TV and digital ads criticizing Dunlap's record at urging voters to support LePage.

Dunlap won the Democratic primary for the state’s 2nd Congressional District, after edging out the party's endorsed candidate, state Sen. Joe Baldacci, in the ranked choice voting tabulation. LePage was unopposed in the GOP primary. 

Republicans are optimistic about flipping the seat in the swing congressional district, which President Donald Trump has won three times. Democrats are hoping to hold onto the seat as part of a broader strategy to win a majority in the U.S. House of Representatives. 

Overall, Musk's PAC has spent more than $8.3 million supporting Republican candidates this election cycle, and has pledged to spend up to $120 million on key congressional races. America PAC spent more than $260 million helping Trump and other Republicans during the 2024 election, according to disclosures.
news.summary: (The Center Square) — The world's “richest man” is pumping money into Maine's congressional races as part of broader efforts to keep control of Congress in Republican hands.

news.title: Some Democrats are recalibrating their approach to transgender issues as they seek a path to power
news.text: California Gov. Gavin Newsom does not like being on Donald Trump's side on any issue. But when it comes to transgender girls and women in sports, particularly at the school level, the Democrat said he largely agrees with the Republican president. Newsom, one of his party's leading White House prospects, believes it's “deeply unfair” for people who are assigned male at birth to compete against girls. “I don’t want to be on that side of it, but I’m being honest — I’d be lying to you if I said differently,” Newsom told the Associated Press as he was campaigning recently in South Carolina. "I haven’t been able to figure out how to make it fair from my perspective.” Newsom is not alone. While most Democratic officials remain steadfast supporters of the transgender community, an increasing number in red and blue states are distancing themselves from their party’s unflinching support for the transgender community’s policy priorities, such as allowing athletes to compete on teams that match their gender identity. The shift follows years of conservative attacks against Democrats on the divisive issue, which affects a relatively small number of transgender people and their families, but has emerged as one of Republicans' most potent political weapons in the Trump era. Soul searching over transgender issues is one facet of a sprawling identity crisis that Democrats are confronting during the midterms and before the next presidential election. Although they risk a backlash from their progressive base, there is also a sense in some corners that the party must evolve on an issue where the overwhelming majority of voters — even many Democrats — agree with Trump. The issue was a central theme for Trump and his Republican allies on the main stage at their midterm convention in Dallas last week, where the president said he hoped Democrats would continue to stand up for transgender girls and women who want to compete in girls' and women's sports. “I’m petrified that they’ll change,” he said. “That will really hurt us.” Republicans are already replaying some of the same political attacks that they used against Kamala Harris in the presidential campaign two years ago, when they said she's “for they/them, not you.” On Friday, they released a new advertisement targeting James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate in Texas, with the same phrase. A political group backed by billionaire Trump ally Elon Musk has begun running digital ads targeting Democrats in key Senate races in Texas, Ohio and Alaska, accusing them of allowing men to compete in women’s sports. In Texas’ pivotal Senate contest, the new ad from Musk’s America PAC opens with a video clip of Talarico saying that “God is nonbinary." Talarico began to distance himself from those positions months ago. He went further in a Fox News interview last week, saying he would vote in favor of a national ban for gender-affirming surgeries for transgender minors, which are rare. “I’ve missed the mark on some of my past statements. I will be the first to admit it,” Talarico said in an interview near the Republican convention site. “I think the reason that politicians in that convention center across the street want to talk about six sexes is because they don’t want to talk about $6 diesel." In Iowa, State Auditor Rob Sand, the Democratic Party's nominee for governor, has spoken out against transgender athletes competing in women's sports as a matter of fairness. Ohio Democratic gubernatorial nominee Amy Acton has taken a similar position, although she has drawn criticism from the left for adopting Trump's language after saying she opposed “boys playing in girls’ sports." And in deep-blue Massachusetts, transgender rights became a defining campaign issue during the state's recent Democratic U.S. Senate primary, illustrating the potential backlash that party members can face. Sen. Ed Markey, 80, secured the nomination and later credited his win to not shying away from advocating for transgender rights. He used the issue to attack his Democratic opponent, Rep. Seth Moulton, who had said he wouldn't want his daughters to play against transgender athletes. Moulton apologized for his comments, which drew outrage from some progressives, but the damage was done. While Moulton lost his primary, his position — not Markey's — is in line with the majority of voters nationally. A June poll from Quinnipiac University found that about 7 in 10 registered voters think that transgender women and girls should not be allowed to play on women’s and girls' sports teams. About one-quarter think they should. Democrats are divided, with about half saying transgender women and girls should be allowed and about half saying they should not. A Pew Research Center poll conducted last year found that just over half, 55%, of Democrats would be “not too” or “not at all” comfortable with athletes playing on teams that don’t match their sex at birth, while 21% said they were “somewhat” comfortable and only 23% said they were “extremely” or “very” comfortable with this. Markey’s public commitment to transgender rights stood out because Democratic politicians are increasingly running away from the issue, said Tyler Hack, executive director of the Christopher Street Project, which is dedicated to electing supporters of transgender rights to federal office. “The reality of being a transgender person in America in 2026 is that on election nights, while other folks are talking about who had a good night and who had a bad night, sometimes you are quietly wondering, ‘Am I going to be OK?’” Hack said. At the same time, even transgender activists are divided over supporting Democrats who have positions that are unfriendly to transgender people. Erin Reed, an advocate and independent journalist covering transgender issues, this month put out a guide flagging Democratic candidates who she accused of taking anti-transgender positions. She highlighted 15 states that have such Democrats, saying that she would not vote for the “worst offenders” even if it means a Republican wins. She doesn’t want Democrats to see that “throwing transgender people under the bus is a winning strategy.” “One seat can be won back,” Reed wrote. “A party cannot.” Meanwhile, Hack would probably vote for a Democrat even if that candidate supports some policies the Christopher Street Project opposes, in hopes that the party can take control of Congress. However, those candidates shouldn't expect the organization's endorsement. “While I hope many of them win, I think they can do it without our resources and without our support," Hack said. The political debate is evolving as transgender people increasingly become the target of conservative backlash through state laws and the Trump administration. Sports participation has become one of the main fronts in a political battle over transgender rights, although most Republican-controlled states have also implemented policies that affect a bigger slice of the population. There are bans on some gender-affirming health care for transgender young people and rules against transgender people from using the bathrooms that match their gender identity in schools and occasionally other public places. At least 25 states are now enforcing laws or policies banning transgender women and girls from competing in at least some women’s and girls' sports and three others have adopted laws but have enforcement blocked by the courts. Earlier this year, the U.S. Supreme Court upheld state laws barring transgender girls from school teams. Transgender athletes make up a small portion of team rosters. NCAA president Charlie Baker testified in 2024 that he knew of fewer than 10 transgender college student-athletes out of more than 500,000 total. The debate within the Democratic Party heading into the 2026 midterms offers a preview for those Democrats contemplating presidential bids in 2028. Newsom, who is considered a frontrunner in the shadow primary, highlighted his long record of supporting LGBTQ+ priorities, including sanctioning same-sex marriage as the San Francisco mayor decades ago and later appointing the first trans judge in California history. But in sports, he thinks it's unfair to allow people assigned as males at birth to compete against girls. “It’s a hard issue. I struggle with it,” Newsom said. “I think people know where my heart is, my soul is. I have a trans godson.” Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker, another likely Democratic presidential contender, has taken the opposite position. He has consistently criticized state-level bans and restrictions on transgender athletes, calling them “bullying” and a “setback for equality.” Following the recent Supreme Court ruling that upheld state bans on transgender athletes, Pritzker, whose cousin is transgender, reaffirmed his position on social media. “There’s a place for you in Illinois,” he wrote. In Pennsylvania, Democratic Gov. Josh Shapiro opposes bans on transgender athletes in school sports, which he's called cruel and designed to discriminate. He argues that athletic participation and eligibility should not be dictated by politicians, but rather handled by local athletic organizations — a stance in line with several LGBTQ+ groups. He's also raised questions of fairness, however. “Look, I think it’s a tough deal being born into the wrong body. And I don’t think these kids deserve to be persecuted and bullied by the president of the United States," Shapiro told The Atlantic last year. "I also don’t think they deserve an unfair advantage on the playing field.” Research has been mixed on whether transgender women have advantages in sports, and it depends partly on whether they went through puberty as boys. Former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, who is gay and a potential presidential contender, said on Fox earlier in the year that he takes people seriously on both sides of the debate “whether you’re talking about parents who are wondering what this means for fairness for their kids competing, or parents who want to make sure that their kids aren’t being discriminated against and get a chance to participate.” “But I also have to tell you,” he added, “I would be surprised if this is a top three or even a top 10 voter issue in the midterms this year." ___ Peoples and Mulvihill write for the Associated Press. AP writers Kimberlee Kruesi in Providence, R.I., and Amelia Thomson DeVeaux in Washington contributed to this report.
news.summary: An increasing number of Democratic leaders have begun to push back against their party’s unflinching support for the transgender community this midterm season.
news.author: Steve Peoples And Geoff Mulvihill
