news.title: James Talarico's Chance of Beating Ken Paxton Flips in New Poll
news.text: Democrat James Talarico holds a narrow lead over Republican Ken Paxton in the state's high-profile U.S. Senate race, according to a recent survey ahead of the November election. The poll, conducted by SoCal Strategies, shows Talarico ahead with 50 percent of the vote compared to Paxton's 45 percent. The figures mark a shift from the pollster's June survey, which had Paxton leading 49 percent to 47 percent. While Texas has long functioned as a Republican stronghold in federal races, shifting demographic and political dynamics have rendered recent cycles increasingly competitive. Newsweek contacted the Talarico and Paxton campaigns for comment by email outside of regular working hours. Talarico Leads Among Most Demographics The survey, carried out between September 12 and 13 among 649 likely voters, indicates that state Representative Talarico commands advantages across multiple voter groups. His support among Hispanic voters grew from 10 percent in June to 38 percent, while his backing among independent voters rose from 10 percent to 45 percent. Among self-identified Republicans, support for the Democratic candidate edged upward to 12 percent, alongside 46 percent among voters aged 18 to 29. Attorney General Paxton maintains advantages among white voters (56 percent to 39 percent), voters aged 45 to 64 (49 percent to 46 percent), and voters over 65 (51 percent to 44 percent). Path to Election Day The poll also signals potential tightening as the election approaches, noting that Republican voters appear more undecided than their Democratic counterparts. "Much like the last poll, Republicans are less decided than Democrats. While six percent of respondents who said they backed Trump in 2024 are currently undecided in the Senate race, the same can only be said of one percent of those who say they voted for [Vice President Kamala] Harris," the survey report noted. "To have a chance, Paxton will need to win nearly all of these voters and peel back a substantial portion of the 12% of Republicans who say they would vote for Talarico if the election were held today." President Donald Trump has thrown his support behind Paxton, calling him the "greatest attorney general in America." He has also repeatedly criticized Talarico, calling him "Talafreako" on social media and in speeches. What Polls Show in the Texas Senate Race Texas has backed Republican presidential nominees in every election since 1980, but Democrats hope 2026 will offer one of their best opportunities in years to compete statewide. Trump carried Texas by 13.7 percentage points in 2024, defeating then-Vice President Kamala Harris 56 percent to around 42.5 percent. Texas has not elected a Democrat to statewide office since 1994, making it one of the nation's longest-running Republican strongholds. Democrats have repeatedly targeted the state as demographic shifts and population growth have reshaped its electorate, but they have fallen short in a series of closely watched campaigns, including Beto O'Rourke's 2018 Senate bid against Ted Cruz. Polls show Paxton and Talarico holding narrow leads at different points in the campaign. The matchup follows Paxton's defeat of longtime Senator John Cornyn in the Republican primary in late May. A YouGov/Univision poll of 1,000 registered voters conducted between August 27-September 4 found Talarico leading by 5 points, 48 percent to 43 percent. It had a margin of error of plus or minus 3.6 percentage points. An Overton Insights/Texas Public Policy Foundation poll of 1,167 likely voters from August 24-26 found Talarico and Paxton locked in a statistical dead heat. The poll found Talarico leading with 44 percent support to Paxton's 43.4 percent, while 12.6 percent of respondents remained undecided. When leaners were included, the race was effectively tied, with both candidates receiving 50 percent support. Other recent polling, such as an Emerson College Polling/Nexstar Media poll of 1,000 likely Texas voters, also puts the Senate race in near deadlock, with 47 percent backing Paxton and 46 percent supporting Talarico. About 5 percent are undecided and 2 percent back a different candidate. The poll was conducted August 9-11 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percentage points. A Fox News poll of 1,006 registered Texas voters found that 51 percent back Talarico and 48 percent Paxton, with 1 percent undecided. The survey was conducted July 23-27 and had a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. Prediction markets reflect the race's razor-thin margins. As of Monday morning, Kalshi showed Talarico at 52 percent and Paxton at 48 percent, while Polymarket gave a slight edge to Talarico at 51 percent compared to Paxton's 50 percent. But once he arrived, things took a turn for the worse.

On Saturday, the Republican made a series of problematic comments he should’ve known to avoid. He slammed NATO. He condemned Joe Biden, Kamala Harris and Illinois Gov. J.B. Pritzker. He questioned the integrity of his own country’s electoral system and accused Democrats of being “communists.” Asked about his recent interaction with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, his response included odd and false claims about the size of the audience at last week’s midterm convention.

In an especially amusing moment, Trump even said first lady Melania Trump was there, before conceding that she was not, in fact, there.

But all of this was soon overshadowed when the president wandered into an international incident of his own making. MS NOW reported:

President Donald Trump said Saturday that he would “love” to see a unified Ireland, setting off strong reactions in the United Kingdom and beyond.

“Well, I don’t want to cause any problems, but I will tell you I’d love to see it unified,” the president told reporters at a meeting with Irish Prime Minister Micheál Martin in Dublin, where residents took to the streets to protest Trump’s visit.

“I think it would be a great thing,” he added. “I mean, how can it be bad?”

In case this isn’t obvious, the underlying issue is deeply complex, and it’s best approached with a nuanced understanding of history, culture, diplomacy and regional politics.

Trump, however, who has long struggled to understand the basics of the relationship between Ireland and the United Kingdom, had no use for any nuances. On the contrary, as the trip continued, he apparently felt the need to lean into his new position, which defied decades of U.S. foreign policy.

news.title: Why Democrats’ blue wave might not be as big as expected
news.text:
The 2026 election will be decided where the wave meets the wall.

Signs are accumulating that the blue wave of Democratic support this year may be even higher than in the 2018 election, when a backlash against President Donald Trump’s tumultuous first term carried the party back into control of the House of Representatives. But the defensive wall that Republicans are constructing against that Democratic tide also looks bigger than in 2018.

The height of the wave gives Democrats legitimate reasons to expect they can win races deep into previously reliably Republican territory. The depth of the wall gives Republicans plausible reasons to hope they can contain their losses to a modest level.

For Democrats, the wave is being powered primarily by turnout and Trump: clear signs that their partisans are more energized than Republicans about voting this year and that voters are now more negative on the president’s performance than not only in 2018, but also in other modern midterms that broke sharply against the party holding the White House, such as 2010 and 2006.

For Republicans, the central bricks in the wall are money and the map: a financial advantage magnified by crucial recent decisions from the Republican-appointed majority on the Supreme Court, and an electoral battlefield that is playing out almost entirely in places Trump carried in 2024.

“This election is home field advantage for Republicans, and they’ve got to exploit that,” says former Republican Rep. Tom Davis, who chaired the National Republican Congressional Committee. “On the other hand, this is a referendum on the president, and he’s had a confluence of very bad things coming together.”

What’s powering the wave

A wide assortment of measures suggests the electoral environment this year is more perilous for Republicans than it was in 2018 — and during other recent midterms that produced significant losses for the party holding the White House.

Those warning lights begin with attitudes about the economy. Compared with 2018, Americans today are much more negative about current economic conditions and much more pessimistic about the future. Inflation has become an inescapable strain on daily life: AAA, for instance, reported that gas prices last week reached $4.28 per gallon, compared with $2.75 on Election Day in 2018 (that’s $3.65 in today’s dollars, factoring for inflation). In the latest CNBC poll this summer conducted by a bipartisan Democratic-Republican pollster team, just 27 percent of Americans described the economy as excellent or good, compared with 73 percent who viewed as fair or poor. In CNBC’s October 2018 poll, 58 percent described the economy in positive terms and only 40 percent in negative ones.

Micah Roberts, a Republican pollster who conducts the CNBC survey with a Democratic partner, says far more Democrats, independents and even Republicans are negative on the economy than in 2018. Just as striking, he says, the share who are not only down on today’s conditions but pessimistic about tomorrow’s is twice as large now as then. “That’s a radically different environment,” Roberts says. “Everybody everywhere is feeling an economic pinch.”

Today’s economic assessment is also gloomier than the results measured in CNBC polls before the midterm election that produced historic losses for Democrats in 2010, and in the exit polls when Republicans lost control of both chambers in 2006.

The Democrats’ 2006 gains were fueled as well by widespread disillusionment over the Iraq War that then President George W. Bush launched in 2003. In the 2006 exit poll, 59 percent of voters said the war had not improved American security — and over three-fourths of those skeptics supported Democrats for the House. Today, the Iran War is facing comparable public opposition in most polls.

Some of Trump’s other initiatives have been more popular, such as his efforts to regain control of the Southern border and the provisions in the “One Big Beautiful Bill” temporarily reducing taxes on tips and overtime. But to a much greater extent than before the 2018 election, Trump has pursued a wide range of other specific policy choices that have provoked opposition from a significant majority of Americans, including his tariffs and the Medicaid cuts in that reconciliation bill.

All of this — especially the economy and the war — has predictably eroded Trump’s support. The negative views of Trump’s economic management “didn’t really exist in 2018,” said Democratic pollster Nick Gourevitch. “2018 was like: ‘He’s a bad guy, crazy guy, but the economy is good.’ Now it’s: ‘He’s a bad guy, crazy guy, and the economy is bad.’”

The latest CNN poll of polls found just 35 percent of Americans approve of Trump’s performance, with 63 percent disapproving. If those levels hold among this November’s electorate, they’ll be much worse than Trump’s standing in the 2018 exit poll, when 45 percent of voters approved and 54 percent disapproved. Trump’s approval rating is also much weaker than that of other presidents in recent midterms when their party suffered losses, including Joe Biden in 2022, Obama in 2010, George W. Bush in 2006 and Bill Clinton in 1994.

Trump’s decline poses a clear and present danger for Republicans: During his first term, Democratic House candidates won 90 percent of voters who disapproved of him in 2018, and 93 percent in 2020, per the exit polls. Likewise, in Senate races over those elections, every Democratic incumbent or challenger except Maine Republican Sen. Susan Collins’ opponent in 2020 won at least 89 percent of voters who disapproved of Trump.

Probably the most worrisome sign for Democrats this year is that many of their candidates are not yet matching those benchmarks among Trump disapprovers. But so many voters now disapprove of Trump — not only in swing states but even such red-leaning places as North Carolina, Texas, Ohio and Georgia — that Democrats can reach 50 percent even with support from fewer of them.

Democratic pollster Anna Greenberg says that in her surveys and focus groups, red-state voters are often the most disenchanted with Trump’s return. They point above all, she says, to inflation, the Iran war and Trump’s focus on his own preoccupations — from making money to gilding the capital with his construction projects.

“In the red states… it feels like independent voters, Hispanic voters, White non-college women to some degree, are really, really angry at Trump,” Greenberg says. “And, in guilt by association, with Republicans. When you do focus groups … they feel betrayed and lied to.”

Whit Ayres, a veteran Republican pollster, says that Trump’s hold remains undiminished on voters who identify as part of his Make America Great Again movement. But he notes, about half of Republican voters don’t identify with MAGA. And among those non-MAGA Republican voters — a group that includes both traditional country-club Republicans and the new, mostly younger and nonwhite, voters Trump attracted in 2024 — Trump “has slipped a lot,” Ayres says.

The turnout gap

Some of those disillusioned 2024 Trump voters (especially people of color) may cross over to vote for Democrats, Ayres and other strategists say. But as American politics have grown more polarized, fewer voters are willing to cross that line. Roberts says that in the CNBC polling, the share of non-MAGA Republicans who say they are still voting for Republicans this fall is about 20 points higher than the portion who approve of Trump’s performance.

“There are a lot of people who may think, ‘I don’t like Trump but … I don’t agree with the policies of the other party and where they would take us,’” Roberts says.

Most analysts agree the biggest risk for the GOP among disillusioned Trump supporters is that they will not vote at all. “That’s one of the major challenges for Republican candidates,” Ayres says. “Democratic enthusiasm is substantially higher than Republican enthusiasm at the moment.”

That potential turnout gap represents the other major component of the possible Democratic wave. Not only do polls consistently show that more Democrats say they are very motivated to vote than Republicans, but more Democrats are voting since 2024.

Political data analyst John Couvillon has calculated that through last week’s New Hampshire contest, 56 percent of all the votes in primaries nationwide this year have been cast in Democratic contests. That’s an even bigger share than their 54 percent in 2018. By contrast, Couvillon found that in 2014 and 2022 — when Republicans made midterm gains — they cast at least 53 percent of primary votes nationwide.

Similarly, Democrats are performing even better in special elections leading into this midterm than they did before 2018. The Downballot, a political website, calculates that in 110 state and federal special elections since 2024, Democratic candidates on average have run 12.5 points better than Kamala Harris did in the same jurisdiction; in 2017 and 2018, Democratic candidates ran 10.6 points better than Hillary Clinton did in 2016.

Two other factors could widen this year’s potential Democratic turnout advantage. One is that across almost all the key battleground states, racial minorities and/or White college graduates, two generally good groups for Democrats, have increased their share of eligible voters since 2018, while Whites without a four-year college degree, the core Trump constituency, have diminished, according to census figures analyzed by demographer William Frey. And while people of color usually make up a smaller share of the vote in midterms than presidential years, the opposite is true for college graduates. These shifts will likely matter only at the margin, but that could be enough to tip some very close races.

The GOP’s bricks in the wall

Amid all these forces churning against them, the Republican wall begins with the map of states and districts at play this year.

Heading into the 2018 election, House Republicans held 23 seats that voted for Clinton two years before and ultimately lost 20 of them. This time, before the redistricting wars, Republicans were defending just three seats that voted for Harris. Looking more broadly, Republicans this year must defend 30 seats that narrowly voted either for or against Trump in 2024, compared with 36 in 2018, according to calculations by the University of Virginia’s Center for Politics. And the GOP’s redistricting drive has left 13 House Democrats defending districts where Trump ran at least 5 points better than his share of the national vote, compared to just four in such districts in 2018. Moreover, fewer House seats overall than in 2018 remain competitive — which leaves Democrats, while still strongly favored to capture the majority, with less room to overcome idiosyncratic stumbles (such as scandals or otherwise vulnerable nominees).

On paper, the Senate map is even more forbidding. Of the Republican-held seats Democrats are most seriously contesting, Maine is the only one in a state that supported Harris; North Carolina is the sole other state on the Senate map where Harris even came close. Trump prevailed by double digits in every other state whose Senate seat Democrats are targeting — Alaska, Ohio, Texas, Iowa, much less Kansas and Nebraska (where Democrats are supporting an independent candidate.)

Even in these states, Trump’s approval has generally fallen into negative territory, which provides Democrats their opening. But to win on this stony soil, Democratic candidates must overcome years of alienation from their national party. In these red states, Democrats “have to establish yourself as a really unique candidate who is going to change the way things are,” says Democratic pollster Celinda Lake. “It isn’t going to be the party that wins; it is going to be a vote for change that wins.”

After the map, money is the next major component of the GOP wall. In 2018, Democratic House and Senate candidates significantly outraised their Republican opponents, according to OpenSecrets.org. And while Republican party committees and independent expenditure groups raised more than their Democratic counterparts that year, that advantage was dulled by federal election rules which limited their direct coordination with campaigns and allowed broadcasters to charge those groups more for ads than they charged candidates.

But two rulings by the Republican-appointed Supreme Court majority this year have swept away those constraints, which will allow Republicans to maximize the big financial advantage their party committees and outside groups have established over their Democratic rivals.

Also working for Republicans is the decline in the Democrats’ own image. In Pew Research polling, favorability ratings for the Democratic Party have hovered in the high 30s for the past three years, a downtick from 2018. But the GOP image is no better-and historically attitudes toward the president in the White House have shaped midterm results much more than views of the party outside it.

Trump’s efforts to tilt electoral rules toward the GOP represent the final section of the GOP wall — the spikes on the battlements. That effort began with his successful pressure on multiple red states to gerrymander their House districts. Still looming are his attempts to restrict mail voting and possible deployments of federal law enforcement at polling places in Democratic areas.

All of this could limit Democratic gains. But strategists in both parties agree that attitudes toward the incumbent president have become the most powerful force influencing midterm outcomes. No wall may be high enough to fully contain the wave of public disenchantment cresting through Trump’s storm-tossed second term.

news.title: Jessica Tarlov shares lessons from being the liberal voice at Fox News in 'I Disagree'
news.text: After appearing last year on a contentious political panel discussion in Washington, D.C., Jessica Tarlov, co-host of the the popular Fox News show "The Five," was approached by a transgender woman from Alabama. Tarlov had said that Democratic candidates in tough races might have to concede that transgender collegiate swimmer Lia Thomas should not be competing against women assigned female at birth. But the matter never came up. Instead, the Alabama woman thanked Tarlov for making the case for Democrats against four conservatives on "The Five," the most watched program in cable news and a favorite of family members who no longer speak to her. "If more people talked like you, I might get my family back," the woman said. "I'm just happy my parents can hear someone like you." Tarlov describes the encounter in her new book "I Disagree: Winning Arguments Without Losing Friends," out Sept. 15. The part how-to book and part personal memoir is aimed at helping readers navigate the harsh political divisiveness in the culture. Her role on "The Five" has made her an advocate of going into not-so-friendly territory to debate issues rather than staying in comfort zones where views are unchallenged. "I’m trying to show that a Democratic voice like mine can exist there, without an apology," she writes of her Fox News position. "And that a person with strong liberal beliefs can bring that same perspective to a host of outlets and places." During a recent conversation at Fox News headquarters in Manhattan, Tarlov said the kind words of the fan from Alabama align with what she's heard from children and grandchildren of the network's loyal viewers. They are grateful their Fox News-loving families are exposed to a voice from outside the conservative media ecosystem. Tarlov, 42, has been a sturdy liberal counterweight at "The Five," which averages 3.5 million viewers daily, according to Nielsen. She comes to the panel's table highly prepared with data-based talking points, forcing her often intractable co-hosts to engage and listen. She often does it while deflecting the mocking remarks of rambunctious colleagues Jesse Watters and Greg Gutfeld, who try to throw off her arguments. "Interruptions are an indication that you're winning," said Tarlov, evoking the pithy chapter summaries in "I Disagree." Tarlov games out numerous scenarios with recommendations on how to deploy statistics and when to lighten up. She also explains the necessity of allowing the other side to blow off steam as she did when "The Five" co-hosts became emotional and overwrought over the shooting of right wing activist Charlie Kirk. Tarlov believes the key to the success of "The Five" is the camaraderie the panel has off-camera. While the co-hosts will battle it out on set over President Trump's policies or the excesses of the socialist wing of the Democratic Party, they are supportive of each other once the show is over (three of them are represented by the same CAA agent). "We don't talk politics outside of work," Tarlov said. Tarlov has been an accepted part of the Fox News family, recently signing a three-year contract despite Trump's suggestion that "The Five" would be better off without her. But it has taken time for Tarlov to gain credibility among like-minded pundits and thought leaders on the political left. Most are dismissive of the network as its most popular hosts are unwavering Trump loyalists. Tarlov also resists being in lockstep with every Democratic position and trend. (She voted for Andrew Cuomo over New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani, citing the former governor's experience.) "Even in the last year I've been at big liberal gatherings, very clearly hosts on other big podcasts or show were not interested in talking to me," said Tarlov, who has had many conversations that start with the question "Why are you on that network?" But with younger news consumers getting their news and information through social media platforms, Fox News clips of Tarlov scoring points for the Democrats are gaining attention. Tarlov said she has felt more welcome in left-leaning circles since the 2024 presidential campaign when the digital accounts of Joe Biden and then Kamala Harris put her commentary in heavy rotation. (Scott Galloway, the author and social critic, partnered with Tarlov on a podcast, "Raging Moderates," after seeing her come up repeatedly in his feeds and then meeting her on the set of "Real Time With Bill Maher"). Tarlov didn't start out seeking a career as a TV personality, although her family background likely helped her understand media and communication. Her parents were attorneys who met while working on the Warner Bros. lot in New York, and raised their two daughters in the hip lower Manhattan neighborhood of Tribeca. Her father, Mark Tarlov, was a onetime speechwriter for Supreme Court Justice Warren Burger who went on to produce two of John Waters' films and direct projects of his own. Tarlov and her sister Molly, an actor who co-starred in the MTV sitcom "Awkward," traveled the world with their father to shooting locations. (Tarlov pays tribute to her father, who died in 2021 of 9/11-related cancer, by wearing his nerd-chic Oliver Peoples eyeglass frames made of buffalo horn). A graduate of Bryn Mawr College and the London School of Economics, Tarlov worked as a strategist on the London mayoral campaign of Boris Johnson. She talked Democratic pollster Doug Schoen into giving her a job. Schoen hired her and brought her to the attention of Fox News, which started using her as a guest on Sean Hannity's program in 2016. The ability to effectively volley with conservatives led Democratic Party leaders to approach Tarlov about running for Congress in the district representing Staten Island. (She has no desire to seek political office.) Tarlov was named co-host on "The Five" in 2022. She and husband Brian McKenna, who works in finance, welcomed their first daughter in 2021, the other in 2024. She remains awed that the show's viewers — most of whom don't agree with her politics — have acknowledged her personal milestones with warm greetings and homemade gifts. She is aware that she's had a rarefied career. But in "I Disagree," she goes beyond her impressive resume to reveal her insecurities — unusual in the ego driven TV news business — and tells readers how she's tried to resolve them. "I have a good amount of shyness to me," she said. "I have a lot of imposter syndrome. I'm constantly in wonder that I ended up getting to do this and that hopefully, am the right person to do it." Long self-conscious about her raspy voice, which Trump once described as "grating and irritating," she shares how a 2016 meeting with former Chief Executive Roger Ailes made her relax about it. He told her viewer criticisms were more aimed at her positions, at not how she sounded. "No matter what room the television is in, you want to make sure the person listening in the next room knows you’re on it," he told her. "Don't try to smooth your voice out. They may hate what you stand for and what you're saying, but you want them to know it's you on TV." Tarlov met with Ailes just months before he was ousted over sexual harassment allegations. While Tarlov was grateful for his advice, her book praises current Fox News Chief Executive Suzanne Scott for creating a workplace culture that is much more hospitable to women. Scott promoted Tarlov to co-host right before she was due to give birth to her first child. "The knowledge that I'm supported allows me to take big swings and not be intimidated," Tarlov writes. She knows that's not the situation for all women; in her signature style, she presents the data and the narrative to back it up.
news.summary: The Democrat that Fox News viewers love to hate offers advice for those uncomfortable political conversations.

news.title: Trump’s easiest path to saving the GOP’s midterms just disappeared
news.text:
At 8:30 a.m. Friday morning, President Donald Trump’s best chance at good economic news before the midterm elections went poof.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that the consumer price index rose in August by 0.4% and 3.4% over the past year. The “core CPI” (the less volatile measure that removes food and energy prices) rose 0.3% for the month and 2.4% annually. For the fifth month in a row, inflation-adjusted wages fell on a yearly basis.

Were this September 2025, the BLS’ report would be disappointing for the White House but hardly catastrophic. Inflation isn’t accelerating, and it remains well below its peak back in 2022. There were even bright spots in some areas: Grocery prices were flat for the second straight month, for instance.

Trump and his party are stuck with the same argument that failed Democrats in 2024: a plea for patience. 

But this is September 2026, and the president and his party are out of time.

This week, the Federal Reserve Board will vote on whether to raise interest rates for the first time since 2023. Trump, who fell out with previous Chairman Jerome Powell over the Fed’s independence, has put enormous pressure on new Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh to lower the rates. The president even threatened to stop trade with countries that have a surplus with the United States if the Fed doesn’t cut rates.

But Warsh has suggested he will disappoint the president.

“Inflation is running above our 2% target,” he said in a speech in Jackson Hole last month. “So the Fed’s predominant focus right now should be on prices.”

As of Friday afternoon, investors put the odds of a rate increase at over 85%. As CNBC’s Matt Peterson wrote, “[Warsh’s] choice now is whether to raise interest rates, or look like he isn’t in control of the central bank he leads.”

A rate increase not only means upward pressure on rates for mortgages, credit cards, car loans and other expenses many voters have; it is also a definitive sign (if another were needed) that Trump’s promise to bring down prices “on Day One” have failed.

For over a year and a half, the White House and its GOP allies have blamed the Biden administration for economic troubles and assured voters that things are getting better.

For instance, consider the $5,000 “dividend” Trump promised this week if Republicans win the midterms. Others at MS NOW have already noted how this stunt is likely illegal on its face, would need congressional approval even if it is legal and mirrors other Trump promises that were never kept.

But there’s also an irony here: These checks may not even cover the pain Trump has brought to people’s pocketbooks.

As my colleague Zeeshan Aleem wrote, “Trump has not only failed to address the cost-of-living crisis with actual solutions, but he’s also systematically made it worse.” Brown University’s Climate Solutions Lab estimated that just at the gas station, the Iran war has cost U.S. households roughly $800 in seven months. And the war has been intensifying again in recent. The Tax Foundation estimated that by the end of 2026, Trump’s tariffs and trade wars will have cost Americans about $1,800 each. Add in higher interest rates and more tax dollars needed to pay for the billions in new military spending and higher debt service costs. Totaled up, as the American Prospect’s Ryan Cooper pointed out, and Trump’s second term “is virtually guaranteed to have cost the average American more than $5,000.”

Even Trump’s promised timing for the checks — after the midterms — is an admission that he and his party are stuck with the same argument that failed Democrats in 2024: a plea for patience. For over a year and a half, the White House and its GOP allies have blamed the Biden administration for economic troubles and assured voters that things are getting better. At times, Trump has even claimed a new golden age is already here.

This month’s inflation report confirms that the GOP’s version of “stick with us” is even harder than it was for Joe Biden in 2022 and later Kamala Harris in 2024. Whereas Democrats could at least say the rate of inflation declined significantly over the latter two years of Biden’s term, that rate has plateaued under Trump — and wages are once again trailing inflation. And to an unusual extent, the president’s actions, most visibly the war with Iran, are to blame, as his polling on the economy shows.

The quickest path to a surprisingly strong midterm for the GOP was through a sharp economic revival. That path is now closed.

news.title: Elon Musk is reusing Trump’s anti-trans strategy. It’s unlikely to work.
news.text:
The world’s richest man is spending at least $100 million on the midterm elections to support the Republican Party and his far-right agenda. But it looks like Elon Musk’s focus won’t be the economy, or the war in Iran or artificial intelligence. It won’t be his repellent ideas about race and his advocacy for “white solidarity.” Instead, Musk has come out of the gate with a barrage of ads targeting Democrats for not being sufficiently supportive of discrimination against transgender Americans.

It’s ugly and hateful, but Musk’s efforts, and those of other Republicans who are sending the same message, will probably fail. 

If the anti-trans ads were brilliantly effective, they should have made a difference in the places where they were run most frequently. But they didn’t.

Two months ago, one Republican operative described the party’s strategy this way: “It’s going to be a hate election.” In fact, that’s a fair description of every Republican campaign going back decades. As Richard Nixon aide Kevin Phillips, the architect of the “Southern Strategy,” said in 1968, “The whole secret of politics is knowing who hates who.” Republicans always have a group they want people to hate. Sometimes it’s immigrants, sometimes it’s Muslims, sometimes it’s uppity women, but there’s always a target.

This year, like the last two years, the GOP has decided the hatred should be directed at trans people, a small and vulnerable group of Americans who already face extraordinary discrimination.

Musk’s transphobia carries a personal motivation: One of his children, a trans woman, has publicly rejected him, and he says she was “killed by the woke mind virus.” And he likely believes that using the anti-trans playbook Donald Trump ran against Kamala Harris in 2024 is the path to success. It’s a common myth, one that never had any empirical support. 

That year Republicans spent $215 million on advertising attacking trans people. After Trump won by 1.5% of the popular vote, the inference that the anti-trans ads made the difference became conventional wisdom. Even now, both inside and outside the GOP, many treat the argument as so self-evidently true it requires no investigation (“Republicans remember how lethal the Trump campaign’s ‘Kamala is for they/them’ ads were to Kamala Harris' campaign in 2024,” Axios recently wrote).

But the assertion that those ads were terribly effective, let alone “lethal” to Harris, has no evidence to support it. No quantitative studies, no analysis of voting patterns showing that places where the ads aired went stronger for Trump, nothing.

When Democrats say, “I support trans rights but I also have concerns” — as too many of them do — they earn no credit. 

There has been little research at all investigating this question. But a randomized trial at the end of the campaign found that while showing voters Trump’s ad produced a small negative effect on sympathy for trans people, “the Trump ad yielded no statistically significant shift in voter choice, mobilization or likelihood to vote.”

That’s not definitive, given that testing ads in a controlled trial doesn’t mirror the way people receive them in the real world. But in that real world, Harris performed better in places where the campaign was most intense on the ground and in the air. If the anti-trans ads were brilliantly effective, they should have made a difference in the places where they were run most frequently. But they didn’t.

In 2025, Republicans tried the anti-trans attacks again, including in the gubernatorial contests in Virginia and New Jersey. Democrats won both contests easily and anti-trans candidates lost local races across the country.

Nevertheless, Musk and his GOP allies are reopening this spigot of hate.

How should Democrats respond? Frightened hedging won’t work. When Democrats say, “I support trans rights but I also have concerns” — as too many of them do — they earn no credit. It only reinforcing the idea that they’re weak and unprincipled., which is the single biggest image problem the Democratic Party faces.

Bans on trans athletes would have to be enforced somehow, such as through invasive (and expensive) DNA testing or gential inspections.

Another answer is to just ignore it, and turn the conversation back what voters actually care about. Poll after poll shows economic concerns swamping every other issue in the campaign.

Or Democrats could choose an approach they seldom take on this issue: Attack. Turn the issue back on their GOP opponents. Let’s consider the issue of trans athletes in sports. A ballot initiative pushed by Republicans in Washington state, for example, requires doctors to verify the sex assigned at birth of every girl who wants play sports. Other GOP-backed bans lack provisions for verifying school athletes’ sex, admitting by omission that any such mechanisms would be unpopular. Before passing a ban in 2021, for example, Florida Republicans removed at the last moment language that would have required transgender athletes in high schools undergo a physical exam and testosterone and genetic testing.

But these bans would have to be enforced somehow, such as through invasive (and expensive) DNA testing or genital inspections. If Democrats were as ruthless as Republicans, they’d be saying things like “I’m worried about how to make life more affordable, but my opponent wants to require genital inspections for little girls. We need to leave kids alone, and tell my opponent to stay out of our kids’ locker rooms.”

Few if any Democrats will do that, of course. But all of them do need to be ready for the nine-figure tsunami of hate Elon Musk is about to unleash on them. They can start by remembering that this campaign from a deeply unpopular tech oligarch is unlikely to succeed. Perhaps knowing that, they’ll realize that standing up against hate is always the right thing to do.

news.title: I am 79 and fitter than most my age. My secret is decades of city cycling
news.text:
Doug Ford’s government is officially taking bids to remove 19 km of bike lanes from Toronto’s streets, Sept. 1

I am an almost 79-year-old grandmother. My bike continues to be my main transportation since moving to Toronto in 1979 — even in winter when there is no snow or ice.

I have not heard anyone talk about the health benefits of cycling. I’m pretty sure it is why I am in better shape than most of my cohort. I feel far safer on the bike because of bike lanes. While I do not live in Etobicoke, I have used the quite lovely lanes that were put there. It will be a travesty if Premier Doug Ford gets his way and has them removed. It is quite frightening that he seems to hate Torontonians in general and cyclists in particular.

Vehicle drivers have no idea how terrifying it is when a vehicle goes too fast and too close to you. I had many such heart stopping moments until bike lanes. The other thing I have done is add some very large artificial flowers to my front and two back carriers. They are bright and easily seen. Research shows that if a driver thinks you are an old woman on a bike, they give a wider berth. This has been my experience, and I also get smiles — even from drivers.

Anne Simmonds, Toronto 

Danielle Smith is a contrarian

Why would Danielle Smith vacation in the U.S., as we fight a trade war with the U. S.? Sept. 9

Alberta Premier Danielle Smith holidays in the U.S. because she can. She is a contrarian and an exceptionalist. Her own narcissism is fed by not being a team player.

Dr. Joy A. Mannette, Toronto 

There are many more extraordinary women to add to this impressive list

Dolly’s gone. Gloria’s gone. The next cool old lady is you, Sept. 6

To Denise Balkissoon‘s impressive list, we should add Margaret Atwood, a quintessentially Canadian voice who’s always been a tough interview and who absolutely nailed the manosphere threat posed by U.S. President Donald Trump in her novel “The Handmaid’s Tale.” I would rather she were on our new $20 bill than King Charles, though no doubt she would demur.

The Women’s Movement and indeed all women, took a body blow when the extraordinarily qualified Hillary Clinton, and then Kamala Harris, lost the elections to an ignoramus, a man who chose equally cruel men for his cabinet (Pete Hegseth, Scott Bessent — who recently compared Canada to a dachshund who needed disciplining by a German shepherd — Howard Lutnick, Stephen Miller — the list goes on.) The women he has surrounded himself are those willing to justify his lies, like Hope Hicks (though she baled early), Pam Bondi, Tulsi Gabbard, Kristi Noem and yes, Karoline Leavitt. The tough Susie Wiles, who called Trump “an alcoholic personality,” has been sidelined. One need not guess what Gloria Steinem, always warm despite her razor-sharp intellect, would think about a UFC match staged on the front lawn of the White House. Fortunately there are tough female intellectuals who are pushing 60 and eloquently nail what’s going on, foremost among whom is Naomi Klein.

Ron Charach, Toronto 

Relying on fossil fuels is a false solution for Canada’s future

There are only 2 ways to win this trade war, and both of them suck. Mark Carney needs to hurry up and pick one, Sept. 9

In his opinion piece Mark McQueen states “Canada could use this money ($100 billion) to build two pipelines east to the Atlantic and two west to the Pacific, plus the LNG plants necessary to get this energy to international markets.” This is totally misguided advice. Most Canadians support climate change solutions.

The federal government’s own report states that “most aspects of Canada’s climate will stabilize in the second half of this century if global CO2 emissions immediately start to decline and reach net zero in the 2070s.” However, the report goes on to say that “climate change will continue to intensify strongly in all regions of Canada if emissions continue to rise throughout the century.”

Relying on an economy based on fossil fuels is a false solution for Canada’s future that will contribute to the climate problem and result in stranded assets as the world moves toward cleaner and less expensive energy solutions. A real solution for our nation’s future is to make major investments in a clean energy grid provided by renewables and energy storage.

Ron Corkum, Mississauga, ON

Municipal hopefuls, let’s hear your determination to tackle an issue that diminishes us all

Ontario municipal elections see modest gains in competition: report, Sept. 9

As the municipal election campaign gears up, let’s have a debate about critical issues affecting civic life, including making city services more efficient and effective. One issue, in particular, stares at us each day if we care to look: homelessness. People who are medically compromised, including those with serious mental illnesses, sleeping on city streets and inhabiting encampments. Today, I called emergency services for an elderly gentleman in obviously very rough shape, sores on his feet, and legs, a wheelchair standing by, and garbage surrounding him. Initially I walked by, but I was compelled to turn around and act. Too often, we, me included, pass these citizens as we go about our day, hardened into what seems to be a reluctant acceptance of this as the new status quo. We shouldn’t accept this inhumanity. It diminishes all of us. Clearly we need a multi-pronged approach, the right housing, wraparound services, better treatment and care for the mentally ill, and the serious involvement of all levels of government to address this insidious and odious stain on all of us. 

So municipal hopefuls let’s hear your plans and dogged determination to tackle this issue.

Desmond Pouyat, Toronto 

Speed bumps provide better safety than speed cameras

A Toronto teen was hit by a car near the site of a removed speed camera. Now his family is suing, Sept. 10

I often drive on a street with several schools and have seen how drivers ignored both the speed limit and speed cameras. Recently the city installed several speed bumps on that same street. The speed bumps do what the cameras never did — they force drivers to slow down which makes the road safer for everyone. If safety is the goal forget speed cameras and, much as I don’t like them, install speed bumps on roads in school districts.

news.title: The 50 races defining the 2026 midterms
news.text:
The last time Republicans faced voters with Donald Trump as president without him also being on the ballot, they lost the House in a rout while gaining Senate seats from friendlier terrain.

Eight years, two presidential elections and one mob assault on the Capitol later, Trump’s hold on the Republican Party is stronger than it was then. Republicans are so bound to him that they staged a midterm convention built around the president and his record — a wager that leans into the one thing midterm voters most reliably punish: the president and the party in power.

Democrats, meanwhile, are still arguing about how they lost to the man they organized their whole strategy against, and whether the way back is through rebuilding the party’s national brand or running from it.

Below are the 50 races that will settle those arguments — starting in a place where Republicans rewrote the rules and may lose anyway.

The Southern state shift

North Carolina Republicans are trying to engineer their way into electoral success by making it harder for a Democrat to keep winning a congressional district coveted by conservatives.

Rep. Don Davis (1) is a moderate who votes against his party often enough — and stays out of the national spotlight thoroughly enough — that he has held his seat even as Democrats have struggled in the South.

* = incumbent

 North Carolina's 1st
 Congressional District

The new lines that GOP lawmakers in Raleigh forced into law, over the objections of a Democratic governor whose power over the map is essentially nil, have made his district friendlier to Trump.

In an ordinary cycle, a shift like that — part of the mid-decade redistricting fight playing out nationally — would have made Davis an easy opponent this fall, especially with Republican Laurie Buckhout challenging him for a second time. But as with so much in the Trump era, the obvious outcome is not the only one possible.

Davis may yet hold on, helped in part by former Democratic Gov. Roy Cooper, who is running against the Trump-backed former Republican National Committee chairman, Michael Whatley, for the state’s open Senate seat. (2)

 North Carolina
 U.S. Senate

Progressives wanted a shot to win in purple places. Now they have it.

For years, Democrats have argued among themselves about whether candidates well to the party’s left can win competitive general elections — with progressives insisting that proximity to the center is not the same thing as electability.

In Michigan, that wing of the party is finally getting a chance to see if its appeal can be broad enough to win over voters in a state Trump has carried twice. A loss by progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed (3) would all but end Democrats’ path to flipping control of the Senate. El-Sayed overcame a fortune in outside spending against him in the August primary, and a victory in November could push the party onto a markedly different course.

 U.S. Senate

Republicans, watching their Senate candidates struggle elsewhere, see former Rep. Mike Rogers as their best chance to take a seat Democrats currently hold. Rogers is two years removed from losing Michigan’s other Senate seat by fewer than 20,000 votes.

The race also runs through some of the country’s rawest divides — over antisemitism and Islamophobia, over U.S. ties to Israel at a moment of deep unease in the Middle East, and over whether “America First” should mean pulling back from the world. Whatever Michigan voters intend by their choice, it will be read nationally as a verdict on all of it.

Progressives have also spent years losing crowded primaries for the right to take on House Republicans. In Michigan’s 7th District, home to the state capital of Lansing, William Lawrence (4) won the nomination to challenge Republican Rep. Tom Barrett, beating both a former U.S. ambassador to Ukraine and a former Navy SEAL who split the field. He did it while answering for past podcast comments in which he, a white leftist, described “the older generation of Black political leadership” as a “pillar, frankly, for establishment capitalist imperialist American power” within the Democratic Party — a dynamic that, he said, “really defangs the white left.”

 Congressional District

Lawrence’s general election pitch may prove a hard sell in a seat Democrats badly want back: Barrett flipped it in 2024 as then-Rep. Elissa Slotkin left to run for U.S. Senate.

House Democrats’ campaign arm picked before voters did. It didn’t get its way.

Control of the House could come down to a handful of seats. Against that backdrop, the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee made its preferences known before primary voters had their say in race in several districts, among them California’s 22nd, Arizona’s 1st and Maine’s 2nd. (5, 6 and 7)

In all three, the candidates the DCCC touted lost to rivals — leaving the winners to campaign with the public knowledge that their own party’s campaign operation had decided against them, whatever shows of support Washington has offered since.

Republicans’ redistricting Hail Mary

Beginning last year, Trump and his allies pursued a nationwide effort to redraw Democratic-held districts in red states, all in service of trying to keep at least a narrow House majority.

Starting in Texas and stretching to Missouri, North Carolina and Florida, GOP-led legislatures changed boundaries in their states to try to bring as many as 11 seats from the left to the right of the chamber this fall. Through that lens, nine races in those states have the potential for an outsize impact: Missouri’s 5th District; Florida’s 9th, 14th, 22nd and 25th; and Texas’ 15th, 28th, 34th and 35th. (8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15 and 16)

That effort got a boost in late April from a Supreme Court ruling described by the Republican Party as “a win for fairness, the rule of law, and anyone who opposes racial gerrymandering.” It opened a path for more Republican-governed states to change districts with major minority populations that had been won by Democrats. Alabama, Louisiana and Tennessee moved quickly as a result, bringing Republicans another trio of potential seats.

Democrats’ attempts to respond to those redraws have been scattered. California Democrats pushed through an overhaul targeting Republicans to offset the Texas gains, but a large-scale effort in Virginia fell apart.

Not every reshaped seat will change hands on election night. But the maps have already altered the fundamentals of the midterms. And there remains a real possibility that Black voters’ anger at seeing their electoral power curtailed across the South — particularly in Alabama’s 2nd District, where Rep. Shomari Figures is running despite the Republican redraw — shows up in turnout. (17)

 Congressional District

The Senate shift to state capitals

Seven years ago, Minnesota Sen. Amy Klobuchar was running for president. 

This fall, she is trying to leave the Senate seat she has held since 2007 to become her state’s governor. (18) The move reflects a clear choice among some politicians: Rather than just be 1 of 100 votes in the Senate, they could lead a state — with all the power, risks and responsibilities that come with it.

 Minnesota Governor

She is not alone. Republican Sens. Tommy Tuberville of Alabama and Marsha Blackburn of Tennessee, both of whom disputed the 2020 presidential election results, are also running to lead their states. (19 and 20)

 Tennessee Governor

 Alabama Governor

 Tuberville

The size of their 2026 wins could springboard them to a White House run

Republicans have a chance this fall to beat Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro in a state that proved pivotal to Trump’s return to the White House.

That doesn’t mean they expect to.

Shapiro faces Republican state Treasurer Stacy Garrity in November, and the potential 2028 presidential contender appears to be running far ahead of her. (21) A decisive win would lift Shapiro higher in a 2028 conversation expected to be enormously crowded.

 Pennsylvania Governor

It could also determine whether his party takes the House.

Pennsylvania has at least three Republican-held congressional seats, and possibly four, where his coattails could matter: Pennsylvania’s 1st, 7th, 8th and 10th districts. (22, 23, 24 and 25) Given how narrow control of the House could end up being, Shapiro’s help could be a force in deciding which party has control of the chamber in Washington at this time next year.

In Georgia, Sen. Jon Ossoff headed into this cycle appearing to be one of the most vulnerable incumbent Democrats in the country. Since then, he has commanded national attention in a race against a Republican challenger whose flaws have led to worry within the GOP. (26) A standout performance from Ossoff, especially coming from the presidential battleground state of Georgia, would only add to talk about him being a strong presidential contender.

 U.S. Senate

Hating on the Democratic Party party could help the left outrun ghosts

Democrats have spent years slipping in Iowa. Since the 2020 caucus debacle cost the state its place at the front of the party’s presidential calendar, the party has struggled. Now it has its best opening in years — in statewide races and down the ballot in a series of House contests, from the Iowa Senate race between Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek and Republican U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson, and the House races in the 1st and 3rd districts. (27, 28 and 29)

Key to Democrats’ efforts is the campaign of state Auditor Rob Sand, the only Democrat holding statewide office in Iowa. He is running for governor while relying on an identity deliberately separate from the national party's — and has shown a willingness to break with it. (30)

 Iowa Governor

The Texas-size question mark

Ken Paxton is among the most controversial candidates on any statewide ballot in the country this fall. The Texas attorney general was impeached, and acquitted, by a legislature run by his own party over allegations that he misused the office. He was also behind the failed Supreme Court bid to overturn Trump’s 2020 loss.

Behind all of that baggage, he still managed to defeat incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in a primary runoff in which the attorney general had Trump’s endorsement.

Democrats have not won a statewide race in Texas since 1994. Paxton’s record has put that streak — and the seat — in genuine peril as he hurtles toward the finish line in a close-fought senate race against state Rep. James Talarico. (31)

 U.S. Senate

Texas is a state where Hispanic voters, who around the nation helped Trump win the presidency, have the ability to secure major electoral influence. In both the Senate race and down the ballot in Texas’ 15th District (see 13, above) — where Bobby Pulido, a famous Tejano musician, is running against incumbent GOP Rep. Monica De La Cruz —immigration politics that were an asset for the right not long ago threaten to turn into a liability.

Election deniers’ path to more power

Republicans have largely tried to move past Trump’s attacks on the 2020 election, even as the president’s false claims that he won have become central to his legacy.

Yet a striking number of election deniers are running for governor this year, several of them well positioned to win — a through line suggesting that siding with Trump on 2020, whatever the falsehoods involved, has carried little political cost.

Voters have generally shown that democracy-related issues are not decisive in their choices. And there is a strong chance that from Florida to Ohio to South Carolina, Republicans who undermined Biden’s 2020 win will hold far more powerful offices heading into the next presidential election. (32, 33 and 34)

 Florida Governor

 Ohio Governor

 South Carolina Governor

Even in states with tougher general electorates, election deniers won their primaries. In Arizona, Rep. Andy Biggs is the GOP nominee for governor after backing Trump’s false 2020 claims, and the party’s nominee for attorney general has amplified stolen-election rhetoric as well. (35 and 36) Meanwhile, Republican Alexander Kolodin, who played a major part in working to throw out 2020 presidential election results in Arizona and award the state to Trump, is running to become its chief elections official. (37)

 Arizona Governor

 Secretary of State

 Attorney General

Georgia’s most important race may not be the one you think

A bruising Republican primary for governor ended with wealthy businessman Rick Jackson defeating the Trump-endorsed candidate, Lt. Gov. Burt Jones, in a June runoff. Jackson has claimed he would be Trump’s “favorite governor.” Jones has declined to endorse him since the primary differences.

No Democrat has won the Georgia governorship since Roy Barnes in the 1998 midterms. If former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms ends that drought, the implications will reach well into the next presidential cycle. Bottoms has a chance to shift her party’s story in the South — and to become the first Black woman elected governor of any state. (38)

 Georgia Governor

 Keisha Lance

The Democrats’ Senate path runs through red states

Whether Democrats can win the Senate depends on persuading voters in states where the party has lost ground.

The path starts with beating Republicans in Maine and in the presidential battleground of North Carolina. Neither is assured — least of all Maine, where allegations against Democrat Graham Platner prompted him to leave the race and forced a candidate switch this summer to former state Senate President Troy Jackson, and GOP Sen. Susan Collins has a formidable record of wins. (39)

 U.S. Senate

If those flips happen, Democrats likely need to win two more states from the grouping of Ohio, Alaska, Texas and Iowa.

Alaska is a real, if surprising, opportunity. Former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola is challenging GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan in a November race, and the state’s ranked-choice ballot could work in her favor. (40)

 U.S. Senate

Ohio is the sorest spot. A state that once decided presidential elections had become red enough by 2020 that the party effectively wrote it off, and it stayed written off in 2024. Former Sen. Sherrod Brown, who lost his seat that year, has drawn real concern from Republicans as an opponent to GOP Sen. Jon Husted. (41) But the party’s position in the state is bleak: Kamala Harris lost Ohio by the widest margin of any presidential nominee of either party there since the 1980s.

 U.S. Senate

House seats are at risk in Ohio too, especially the one held by longtime Rep. Marcy Kaptur. She has frustrated Republicans for years by hanging on, but a rematch against Republican Derek Merrin — in a district made more winnable for conservatives by last year’s bipartisan redistricting compromise — sets up a tense fall. (42)

 Congressional District

The new Democratic coalition that leadership could face

At least five democratic socialists are expected to win easily this fall and arrive in Congress: Chris Rabb in Pennsylvania, Melat Kiros in Colorado, Donavan McKinney in Michigan, and Claire Valdez and Darializa Avila Chevalier in New York. (43, 44, 45, 46 and 47)

If Democrats flip the chamber, that bloc could be a problem for House leadership. Republicans’ narrow majority these past few years has shown how much leverage a handful of members on a party’s flank can wield over its leaders.

The Bernie Sanders Blue Dogs

Democrats’ internal divisions are deep — over policy, over how to use power, over who is to blame for losing. But in a few places, the two forces pulling at the party are centered in the same direction.

Just a few House candidates have managed in these midterms to be both endorsed by progressive Sen. Bernie Sanders and the Blue Dog political outfit synonymous with centrism: Brian Poindexter in Ohio, running against controversial incumbent Republican Rep. Max Miller (48); Sam Forstag, who has worked as a smokejumper and is trying to win in Montana (49); retired firefighter Bob Brooks in Pennsylvania (see 23, above); and Rebecca Cooke, a returning candidate in Wisconsin, where she faces Rep. Derrick Van Orden. (50)

Their races run from difficult efforts to frontline contests that control of Washington may turn on. Together, they also suggest how a party fractured by its own arguments can learn from candidates trying to meet the moment for voters who feel Democrats either misled them or did too little when they had the chance.
